title: Hard-negative vocabulary training for open-vocabulary detectors
one_line_idea: Train open-vocabulary detectors with explicitly mined confusable negative class names so that inference-time vocabulary expansion stops silently destroying precision.
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors are trained to align regions with positive class names, but at deployment the user supplies arbitrary vocabularies containing near-synonyms and confusable concepts the model never saw as negatives, so precision collapses in ways training never measured.
core_hypothesis: The dominant failure mode of vocabulary expansion is not missing knowledge but the absence of contrastive pressure between semantically adjacent names, which a hard-negative name mining objective can supply without new box labels.
core_claim: Adding a text-side hard-negative contrastive term, with negatives mined from embedding neighbors of each ground-truth class name, improves precision under vocabulary expansion at equal recall without any additional annotation.
method_sketch: For each annotated region, retrieve top-k nearest neighbor concept names from a large noun inventory using the text encoder, filter out true synonyms with a lexical resource, and add them as explicit negatives in the region-text contrastive loss; evaluate with progressively enlarged inference vocabularies.
falsifiable_prediction: A detector trained with mined name negatives will lose substantially less average precision than a standard-trained twin when the inference vocabulary is grown from tens to thousands of names, with the gap widening monotonically in vocabulary size.
why_important: Real deployments of open-vocabulary detection use large user-defined vocabularies, and silent precision collapse under vocabulary growth is a direct blocker for practical use.
why_possibly_novel: Hard negatives are standard in retrieval, but systematic name-space negative mining as a training signal for detection vocabulary robustness appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat the class-name space, not the image space, as the place where hard negatives must be mined for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train two identical open-vocabulary detector heads on the same base-class split, one with mined name negatives, and compare precision-recall as the evaluation vocabulary is expanded in controlled increments.
main_risk: Synonym filtering may be unreliable, so some mined negatives are actually correct labels and the loss teaches the model to reject true names.
kill_risk: If precision under vocabulary expansion is unchanged or worse with name negatives, the core mechanism is refuted.
community_default_belief: Open-vocabulary detection quality is mainly limited by the scale and quality of region-text pretraining data, and larger vocabularies mostly work if the text encoder is good.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive pretraining gives coarse alignment but never optimizes decision boundaries between adjacent names for the same region, so the failure is an objective gap, not a data-scale gap.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Take a pretrained open-vocabulary detector, expand the vocabulary with embedding-neighbor distractor names on a small validation set, and check whether precision drops sharply; if it does not, the premise is already wrong.

title: Prompt-paraphrase variance as a free calibration signal for novel classes
one_line_idea: Use the variance of detection scores across paraphrased text prompts as an unsupervised confidence signal that flags false positives on unseen classes.
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors output uncalibrated scores for novel classes, and there is no labeled data on which to calibrate them, so downstream thresholds set on seen classes transfer badly.
core_hypothesis: Score instability under prompt paraphrase correlates with prediction error on novel classes, because correct groundings are supported by many phrasings while spurious alignments are phrasing-specific.
core_claim: A variance-penalized score computed from a handful of automatic paraphrases yields materially better novel-class precision-recall tradeoffs than the raw single-prompt score, with no labels required.
method_sketch: Generate several paraphrases per query name with a language model, run the detector per paraphrase or batch the text embeddings, compute mean and variance of per-box scores after box matching across prompts, and rescore boxes with a mean-minus-lambda-times-variance rule tuned only on seen classes.
falsifiable_prediction: On held-out novel classes, ranking detections by variance-penalized score will strictly dominate ranking by raw score across most of the precision-recall curve.
why_important: Calibration on unseen concepts is the practical bottleneck for open-vocabulary deployment where no validation labels exist by definition.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ensembling for accuracy is common, but exploiting cross-prompt disagreement as an error detector for novel-class boxes appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Disagreement across phrasings is an unsupervised proxy for grounding correctness.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one open-vocabulary benchmark split, compute per-box cross-paraphrase variance for novel classes and test whether it separates true from false positives better than raw score using a simple ROC comparison.
main_risk: Paraphrase quality may be inconsistent across concept types, making the variance signal noisy exactly for rare, hard-to-paraphrase concepts.
kill_risk: If cross-prompt variance is uncorrelated with correctness on novel classes, the entire signal is dead.
community_default_belief: Prompt ensembling is a small averaging trick that improves scores slightly, and calibration for novel classes fundamentally requires labeled data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The ensemble contains second-moment information the community throws away by averaging, and that discarded information may be precisely what calibration needs.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One afternoon-scale run: score a few thousand novel-class detections under five paraphrases each and compute the correlation between variance and correctness.

title: Concept-frequency-stratified evaluation for open-vocabulary detection
one_line_idea: Stratify open-vocabulary detection evaluation by how frequently each so-called novel concept appears in web-scale pretraining text, exposing how much claimed openness is just pretraining familiarity.
problem: Benchmarks label classes as novel because they lack box annotations, but the underlying concepts may be abundant in image-text pretraining corpora, so reported novel-class performance conflates true generalization with concept familiarity.
core_hypothesis: Novel-class detection accuracy is strongly predicted by concept frequency in the pretraining corpus, and performance on genuinely rare concepts is far lower than headline novel-class numbers suggest.
core_claim: A frequency-stratified evaluation protocol, with concept frequency estimated from public corpus statistics or corpus proxies, will reveal a steep performance gradient that current aggregate metrics hide.
method_sketch: Estimate a frequency proxy for each evaluation concept from an accessible text corpus or n-gram resource, bucket novel classes by frequency, report per-bucket detection metrics, and release the stratification as an evaluation artifact.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-bucket average precision on novel classes will decrease monotonically with decreasing concept frequency, with the lowest-frequency bucket dramatically below the aggregate novel-class number.
why_important: If openness claims are mostly familiarity, the field is over-reporting generalization and practitioners will be misled about long-tail deployment readiness.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-stratified analysis exists for classification and language tasks, but a standardized frequency-stratified protocol for open-vocabulary detection benchmarks appears missing (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Redefine novel to mean rare-in-pretraining rather than unannotated-in-benchmark.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one open-vocabulary detector and one benchmark, compute a corpus-frequency proxy per novel class, and regress per-class average precision on log frequency; a strong positive relationship supports the reframing.
main_risk: Frequency proxies from accessible corpora may mismatch the actual closed pretraining data of a given model, weakening the analysis.
kill_risk: If per-class accuracy shows no meaningful relationship to any reasonable frequency proxy, the stratification adds nothing.
community_default_belief: Benchmark novel classes measure open-vocabulary generalization because the detector never saw boxes for them.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Box supervision is not the only supervision channel; text-side exposure can carry most of the information, making the box-based novelty definition nearly vacuous.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate per-class novel average precision with word frequency in a public corpus for a single released detector; the correlation coefficient answers the question in hours.

title: Context-ablated region embeddings to fight co-occurrence bias in open-vocabulary detection
one_line_idea: Force region embeddings to remain predictive when the background is masked out, so open-vocabulary detectors stop naming regions by their context instead of their content.
problem: Region features inherited from image-level vision-language pretraining encode surrounding context, so detectors label a region by what co-occurs with it, producing systematic confusions like naming the rider when boxing the bicycle.
core_hypothesis: A consistency loss between full-context and background-masked region embeddings reduces co-occurrence-driven misclassification without harming cases where context is legitimately needed.
core_claim: Context-ablation consistency training measurably reduces confusion between frequently co-occurring category pairs at negligible cost to overall accuracy.
method_sketch: During training, compute region embeddings twice, once normally and once with pixels outside the box blurred or masked, and add a loss aligning the two embeddings plus keeping classification correct under masking; evaluate on a curated confusion set of co-occurring pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: The confusion rate on high-co-occurrence category pairs will drop relative to a control model, while accuracy on context-dependent small objects will drop by less than the co-occurrence gain.
why_important: Co-occurrence shortcuts are a core reliability failure for open-vocabulary detection in scenes that differ from web-photo statistics, such as robotics and industrial imagery.
why_possibly_novel: Context ablation is known in classification analysis, but using it as a training-time consistency constraint specifically for region-text alignment appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Make the region embedding answer what is inside the box, on pain of a consistency penalty.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one detector with and without the masking consistency term and compare error matrices restricted to the top co-occurring category pairs on a standard benchmark.
main_risk: Masking artifacts may themselves become a distribution shift that degrades the backbone features in unpredictable ways.
kill_risk: If co-occurrence confusions persist unchanged under the consistency loss, the bias lives deeper in the text encoder and this intervention dies.
community_default_belief: Better and bigger region-text pretraining will naturally resolve context confusions because the alignment gets finer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web supervision itself is contextual, since captions describe scenes rather than crops, so scale reinforces rather than removes the co-occurrence prior.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an existing detector on boxes with background masked at inference only; if predictions barely change, context dependence is small and the premise fails fast.

title: Decomposed attribute-noun scoring for compositional open-vocabulary queries
one_line_idea: Score compound queries like a red suitcase with separate attribute and noun heads combined explicitly, instead of trusting a single region-text similarity that collapses composition.
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors handle single nouns reasonably but fail on attribute-object compositions, often returning any suitcase for red suitcase, because a single similarity score cannot verify both constituents.
core_hypothesis: Composition failures stem from the scoring function, not the features; the same region features scored by separate attribute and noun projections combined multiplicatively recover much of the lost compositionality.
core_claim: A lightweight decomposed scoring head retrofitted onto a frozen open-vocabulary detector improves compound-query precision substantially with no backbone retraining.
method_sketch: Parse queries into attribute and head-noun parts, learn two projection heads on frozen region features supervised with automatically color-and-texture-augmented pseudo-labels, and score as the product of calibrated constituent probabilities.
falsifiable_prediction: On a compound-query test set built from existing attribute annotations, decomposed scoring will raise precision at fixed recall relative to holistic similarity scoring by a clear margin.
why_important: Compositional queries are the main practical interface for open-vocabulary detection in search and robotics, and current failure rates make the feature untrustworthy.
why_possibly_novel: Compositionality is studied in vision-language retrieval, but retrofit-time decomposed scoring for detection queries appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Fix composition at the scoring head, treating the frozen detector as a feature oracle.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build compound queries from an attribute-annotated detection dataset, evaluate holistic versus decomposed scoring on identical frozen features, and compare precision-recall curves.
main_risk: Frozen region features may simply not encode attributes well enough for any scoring scheme to recover them.
kill_risk: If linear probes cannot decode attributes from frozen region features above chance, the retrofit approach is dead on arrival.
community_default_belief: Compositional grounding failures require retraining with compositional supervision at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information may already be present in the features and lost only in the final dot-product bottleneck, which is fixable cheaply after the fact.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Linear-probe frozen region features for a handful of attributes; probe accuracy immediately bounds what any decomposed head can achieve.

title: Per-concept learned temperature for vocabulary-size-robust scoring
one_line_idea: Replace the shared softmax temperature in open-vocabulary detection with a per-concept temperature predicted from the text embedding, so score calibration survives vocabulary growth.
problem: Detection scores computed against a text-embedding classifier shift systematically as vocabulary size changes, because a single temperature cannot serve concepts with very different embedding-space neighborhood densities.
core_hypothesis: A concept name embedded in a dense semantic neighborhood needs a different score sharpness than an isolated one, and this required temperature is predictable from text-embedding geometry alone.
core_claim: A small network mapping text-embedding neighborhood statistics to per-concept temperatures yields detection scores whose operating thresholds transfer across vocabularies of very different sizes.
method_sketch: Compute per-concept features such as local embedding density and neighbor margins, train a temperature-prediction head jointly with the detector on random vocabulary subsets of varying size, and evaluate threshold transfer from small to large vocabularies.
falsifiable_prediction: A threshold tuned on a small vocabulary will retain far more of its intended precision when the vocabulary is scaled up under learned per-concept temperatures than under a single global temperature.
why_important: Practitioners tune thresholds once and then edit vocabularies constantly; threshold non-transfer is a silent production failure mode.
why_possibly_novel: Per-class calibration exists, but predicting calibration parameters from text-embedding geometry so they extrapolate to unseen concepts appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Calibration parameters as a function of concept geometry, not a per-class lookup table.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with random vocabulary subsampling plus the temperature head, then measure precision drift at a fixed threshold while sweeping inference vocabulary size against a global-temperature control.
main_risk: Embedding-geometry features may be too weak a signal, making the learned temperatures collapse to a constant.
kill_risk: If precision drift under vocabulary growth is identical with and without the head, the mechanism is falsified.
community_default_belief: Score calibration in open-vocabulary detection is a post-hoc nuisance handled by tuning a single threshold per deployment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The threshold that works depends on the vocabulary composition itself, so no single post-hoc constant can be correct across edits.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure how the score distribution of a fixed concept shifts as distractor names are added; if the shift is negligible, the problem this solves does not exist.

title: Semantic drift audit for open-vocabulary pseudo-labeling loops
one_line_idea: Quantify and correct the concept drift that accumulates when open-vocabulary detectors generate pseudo-boxes used to train the next detector generation.
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors increasingly bootstrap training data for themselves and successors, but each generation redefines concepts slightly, and nobody measures whether the meaning of a class name drifts across pseudo-labeling generations.
core_hypothesis: Iterated pseudo-labeling causes measurable semantic drift, where concept boundaries contract toward easy prototypes and expand along systematic error directions, degrading exactly the rare visual variants that motivated open vocabulary.
core_claim: A drift metric based on embedding distributions of pseudo-labeled instances across generations predicts downstream rare-variant recall loss, and anchoring each generation with a small frozen human-labeled set arrests the drift.
method_sketch: Run two or three self-training generations, track per-class instance-embedding distributions and their divergence across generations, correlate divergence with per-class recall changes on held-out human labels, and test a small anchor-set regularizer.
falsifiable_prediction: Classes with higher cross-generation embedding divergence will show larger drops in recall on human-verified rare variants, and anchored training will reduce both divergence and the recall drop.
why_important: Self-training pipelines are becoming the default data engine for detection, and unmeasured drift compounds silently across model generations.
why_possibly_novel: Model-collapse-style analyses exist for generative models, but a concrete drift metric and anchoring protocol for detection pseudo-labeling loops appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat class meaning as a distribution that self-training moves, and measure the motion.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two generations of self-training on one dataset, tracking per-class embedding divergence and human-labeled recall for a handful of classes with known visual diversity.
main_risk: Drift may be too small over feasible generation counts to measure, even if it matters at industrial scale.
kill_risk: If embedding divergence is uncorrelated with any recall change, the proposed metric is useless.
community_default_belief: Pseudo-labeling with a strong teacher is a reliable data amplifier whose errors average out with scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Errors are systematic rather than random, so amplification compounds them directionally rather than averaging them away.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare instance-embedding distributions of teacher pseudo-labels versus human labels for the same class on the same images; a large immediate gap indicates drift pressure exists.

title: Part-whole consistency constraints for open-vocabulary detection
one_line_idea: Add an inference-time consistency layer that uses part-whole relations between query concepts to stop detectors from boxing a part when asked for the whole and vice versa.
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors confuse parts and wholes, returning a wheel for the query bicycle or a whole animal for the query paw, because region-text similarity has no notion of mereology.
core_hypothesis: Many part-whole errors are geometrically detectable, since a part box for a whole query is typically contained inside a high-scoring box of the whole concept, and a relation-aware rescoring can exploit this.
core_claim: A post-hoc rescoring pass that queries both the concept and its known parts or wholes, then penalizes containment-inconsistent detections, reduces part-whole confusions without retraining.
method_sketch: Build a small mereology map for evaluation concepts from lexical resources, run auxiliary queries for related parts and wholes, detect containment patterns between candidate boxes, and rescore detections violating expected containment direction.
falsifiable_prediction: On a curated part-whole confusion set, relation-aware rescoring will cut confusion errors substantially while leaving accuracy on unrelated classes essentially unchanged.
why_important: Part-whole errors are common, embarrassing, and particularly harmful for robotic grasping and inspection where the box extent drives physical action.
why_possibly_novel: Mereological consistency has been studied in segmentation and knowledge bases, but as an inference-time rescoring layer for open-vocabulary detection it appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Use containment geometry plus a lexical part map as a zero-training consistency checker.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate a few hundred part-whole confusable query cases from existing annotations, apply the rescoring layer to a frozen detector, and measure the confusion-specific error rate change.
main_risk: Auxiliary part queries may themselves be unreliable, injecting new errors that offset the corrections.
kill_risk: If containment patterns do not distinguish correct from confused detections in practice, the geometric signal is insufficient.
community_default_belief: Part-whole confusion is a long-tail semantics problem that only richer pretraining data can fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The needed disambiguating evidence is already present in the detector output geometry and merely requires a relational read-out.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For a frozen detector, query a handful of whole concepts and their parts on one dataset and inspect containment statistics of correct versus confused boxes.

title: Isolating the naming bottleneck in open-vocabulary detection
one_line_idea: Experimentally decompose open-vocabulary detection into class-agnostic localization and region naming to establish which is the real bottleneck, then attack naming with retrieval augmentation.
problem: The field improves open-vocabulary detectors end to end without knowing whether novel-class failures come from not finding the object or from not naming it, which makes method design blind.
core_hypothesis: Class-agnostic localization transfers well to novel classes while naming accounts for most of the novel-class error, implying that retrieval-augmented naming should beat further localization work.
core_claim: An oracle study will show that giving perfect names to predicted boxes recovers most novel-class performance, and a k-nearest-neighbor naming head over a visual memory of exemplar crops captures a large share of that headroom.
method_sketch: Run a class-agnostic proposal evaluation on novel classes to measure localization recall, then evaluate naming accuracy given ground-truth boxes, then insert a retrieval head that names regions by nearest exemplars in a growing memory bank.
falsifiable_prediction: Proposal recall on novel classes will be far higher than end-to-end novel average precision, and the retrieval naming head will close a meaningful fraction of the gap without retraining the localizer.
why_important: Correct bottleneck attribution redirects the research effort of a whole subfield toward the component that actually limits performance.
why_possibly_novel: Individual pieces exist, but a controlled decomposition with a retrieval-based remediation quantified against the oracle headroom appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Measure the naming-versus-locating split before proposing anything else.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one benchmark, compute novel-class proposal recall, oracle-name average precision, and retrieval-head average precision for a single frozen detector.
main_risk: The decomposition may be benchmark-specific, with different bottlenecks on different data distributions.
kill_risk: If localization recall on novel classes is actually low, the entire naming-centric program collapses.
community_default_belief: Novel-class failure is a joint problem best addressed by scaling region-text pretraining end to end.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectness may be nearly class-universal already, making end-to-end scaling an expensive way to fix only the naming half.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate class-agnostic box recall of an existing detector on novel classes; a single number decides which half of the pipeline is broken.

title: Cross-lingual parity audit and distillation for open-vocabulary detection
one_line_idea: Measure how much open-vocabulary detection degrades for non-English queries and close the gap by distilling English-query outputs into a multilingual text tower.
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors are overwhelmingly trained and evaluated with English queries, and their behavior under translated queries is unmeasured, likely leaving most of the world with a degraded product.
core_hypothesis: Detection performance drops significantly for typologically distant languages, and self-distillation using machine-translated query pairs on unlabeled images recovers most of the gap without box labels.
core_claim: A parity benchmark built by professionally translating query sets, plus a distillation loss aligning per-box scores across query languages, substantially reduces cross-lingual detection disparity.
method_sketch: Translate benchmark class names into a diverse language set, quantify per-language performance gaps, then fine-tune the text tower so translated queries reproduce the per-box score distributions of English queries on unlabeled images.
falsifiable_prediction: Score-alignment distillation will recover the majority of the measured per-language average-precision gap for languages where the initial gap is large.
why_important: Language equity in vision systems is both an adoption issue and a fairness issue, and detection has escaped the multilingual scrutiny applied to language models.
why_possibly_novel: Multilingual vision-language work exists for retrieval and classification, but a detection-specific parity audit with per-box score distillation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Per-box cross-lingual score alignment as label-free multilingual supervision.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one open-vocabulary detector on one benchmark with translated class names in several languages and quantify the gap; then run the distillation on a subset and re-measure.
main_risk: Translation ambiguity for fine-grained categories may contaminate both the audit and the distillation targets.
kill_risk: If per-language gaps are already negligible, the problem is smaller than assumed and the project reduces to a null report.
community_default_belief: Multilingual text encoders inherited from pretraining make query language a non-issue for detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection scoring depends on fine-grained embedding geometry that multilingual alignment at the sentence level does not guarantee at the concept level.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run one detector with class names in three languages on one validation set and compare mean average precision; hours of compute, immediate answer.

title: Label-free temporal stabilization for open-vocabulary video detection
one_line_idea: Enforce query-conditioned temporal consistency of open-vocabulary detections across neighboring video frames as a training signal, eliminating flicker without any video annotations.
problem: Frame-wise open-vocabulary detectors flicker badly on video, with objects appearing and disappearing across adjacent frames under the same query, and video box annotation for open vocabularies is prohibitively expensive.
core_hypothesis: Temporal instability reflects decision-boundary noise rather than genuine evidence change, so a consistency loss between tracked regions in unlabeled video will improve single-frame reliability as well as temporal stability.
core_claim: Self-supervised fine-tuning on unlabeled video with a track-consistency objective reduces detection flicker substantially and also improves still-image accuracy near decision boundaries.
method_sketch: Run a frozen detector plus a lightweight tracker on unlabeled video, mine tracks with high-confidence majority labels, penalize per-frame score deviations along tracks, and fine-tune with a small learning rate to preserve base capabilities.
falsifiable_prediction: Flicker metrics on held-out video will improve markedly, and still-image benchmark accuracy will not degrade but improve slightly for borderline-score instances.
why_important: Video is the dominant deployment medium for detection, and temporal instability destroys user trust and downstream tracking quality.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal consistency is standard in video segmentation, but as a label-free fine-tuning signal specifically for open-vocabulary query-conditioned detection it appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Tracks as free supervision for query-conditioned score stability.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one detector on a small unlabeled video corpus with the consistency loss and measure flicker rate and still-image accuracy against the frozen baseline.
main_risk: Tracker errors may propagate wrong majority labels along tracks, teaching confident mistakes.
kill_risk: If flicker reduction comes entirely at the cost of still-image accuracy, the method is a smoothing trick rather than a learning signal.
community_default_belief: Video stability is a post-processing problem solved by temporal smoothing or tracking on top of a fixed detector.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Post-hoc smoothing hides but does not fix boundary noise, whereas training against the inconsistency can actually move the decision boundary to a stabler place.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Quantify how much detector score variance along ground-truth-stable tracks exceeds variance expected from appearance change; if scores are already stable, there is nothing to fix.

title: Separate conformal calibration groups for seen and unseen classes in mixed vocabularies
one_line_idea: Calibrate open-vocabulary detectors with distinct conformal adjustment for seen versus unseen concepts so seen classes stop monopolizing mixed-vocabulary inference.
problem: When seen and unseen classes compete in one vocabulary, seen classes systematically dominate scores, suppressing correct unseen-class detections in a way single-threshold calibration cannot repair.
core_hypothesis: The seen-unseen score gap is a stable, estimable bias, and applying group-wise conformal score adjustment with seen-class data plus a small audit set restores balanced ranking without retraining.
core_claim: Group-conditional conformal calibration yields higher harmonic-mean performance across seen and unseen classes than any single global threshold or temperature applied to the same detector.
method_sketch: Estimate score distributions for seen classes from validation data and for unseen classes from a small human-verified audit sample, compute group-wise conformal quantiles, and rescore detections so cross-group score comparisons become meaningful.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched total detection budgets, group-calibrated scoring will recover substantially more unseen-class true positives while losing few seen-class true positives compared with global calibration.
why_important: Mixed vocabularies are the realistic setting, and seen-class dominance quietly converts an open-vocabulary system into a closed one at deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal methods are spreading in vision, but group-conditional conformal correction targeted at the seen-unseen asymmetry in detection scoring appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat seen versus unseen as calibration groups with provable per-group coverage.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a benchmark with seen-unseen splits, compare global versus group-wise calibrated scoring for the same detector, measuring per-group recall at a fixed combined false-positive budget.
main_risk: The unseen-class audit sample may be too small or unrepresentative, making the unseen-group quantile estimate unstable.
kill_risk: If the seen-unseen score bias varies wildly per concept rather than being group-stable, group-level correction cannot work.
community_default_belief: A single confidence threshold per deployment, possibly with temperature scaling, is adequate calibration for detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The score distributions of seen and unseen concepts differ structurally, not just in scale, so no single monotone transform can align both at once.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Plot score histograms of correct detections for seen versus unseen classes for one detector; a visible distributional gap validates the premise in an afternoon.

title: Size-adaptive localization criteria to replace IoU for tiny objects
one_line_idea: Replace intersection-over-union with a size-adaptive localization criterion in both matching and evaluation, because a one-pixel error destroys IoU for tiny boxes while being physically irrelevant.
problem: IoU between small boxes is hypersensitive to pixel-level jitter, so training assignment and evaluation both punish tiny-object predictions for errors below the annotation noise floor, distorting learning and reported progress.
core_hypothesis: A criterion that normalizes localization error by object size plus an absolute-pixel tolerance floor will change which predictions count as correct for small objects, and training with matching based on it will improve small-object detection under human judgment.
core_claim: Swapping IoU for a size-adaptive criterion in assignment and in evaluation improves small-object average precision as judged by human-acceptability studies, while leaving large-object behavior unchanged.
method_sketch: Define a matching score with a normalized center-distance and size-error term and a pixel-tolerance floor, retrain a standard detector with assignment under this score, and evaluate with both classic IoU-based metrics and human acceptability ratings of matched boxes.
falsifiable_prediction: Detectors trained with the size-adaptive criterion will be preferred by human raters on small objects at a clear rate over IoU-trained twins even when classic IoU metrics show little difference.
why_important: Small-object detection drives aerial, medical, and inspection applications, and the field may be optimizing a metric artifact rather than task quality.
why_possibly_novel: Alternative localization losses exist, but coordinating a tolerance-floored size-adaptive criterion across assignment, loss, and human-validated evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The metric, not the model, may be the small-object bottleneck.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrain one detector on one aerial or small-object dataset with size-adaptive matching, then run a small human study comparing accepted detections against the IoU-trained control.

title: Estimating and exploiting the annotation noise floor for small-object regression
one_line_idea: Measure the per-size annotation noise floor with repeated labeling and use a noise-aware regression loss that stops trying to fit residuals below that floor.
problem: For small objects, human box jitter can rival or exceed model localization error, so standard regression losses spend capacity fitting annotator noise and gradients near convergence are mostly noise.
core_hypothesis: Injecting a size-dependent noise model into the regression likelihood, with variance estimated from multi-annotator data, improves small-object performance and training stability by discounting sub-noise residuals.
core_claim: A heteroscedastic regression loss with empirically calibrated size-dependent label variance outperforms standard L1-style losses on small objects and is insensitive to late-training learning-rate choices.
method_sketch: Collect or reuse repeated annotations on a subset to fit a variance-versus-size curve, plug it into a Gaussian or Laplace likelihood for box regression as fixed label noise, and retrain standard detectors.

kill_risk: If model localization error is still far above the annotation floor, discounting sub-floor residuals changes nothing and the premise is void.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Ground truth is a distribution, not a point, and for tiny boxes its spread is large enough that point-fitting is actively harmful.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare state-of-the-art model localization error against inter-annotator disagreement on the same small-object subset; if model error is much larger, park the idea.

title: Anti-aliased downsampling as a targeted fix for small-object feature destruction
one_line_idea: Audit how much small-object information is destroyed by aliasing in strided downsampling and test whether anti-aliased stems and pyramids specifically recover small-object detection.
problem: Backbone downsampling with strided convolutions and pooling aliases high-frequency content, and small objects live almost entirely in exactly the frequencies that aliasing corrupts, yet detection backbones are rarely designed with sampling theory in mind.
core_hypothesis: A significant fraction of small-object misses originate at the first few downsampling layers, and low-pass-filtered downsampling recovers a disproportionate share of small-object recall at negligible cost elsewhere.
core_claim: Replacing standard strides with blur-pooled equivalents in the early backbone improves small-object average precision meaningfully more than it changes medium and large object metrics.
method_sketch: Instrument feature maps to measure small-object signal energy surviving each downsampling stage, swap in anti-aliased downsampling variants stage by stage, and attribute small-object metric changes to specific stages.
falsifiable_prediction: Anti-aliasing the earliest stages will yield the largest small-object gains, and the gain profile across stages will track the measured signal-destruction profile.
why_important: If true, a cheap architectural hygiene fix recovers performance that the field currently buys with expensive resolution increases.
why_possibly_novel: Anti-aliased networks exist for classification shift-invariance, but a stage-wise signal-survival audit tied to small-object detection outcomes appears underexplored (novelty not verified).

minimal_falsification_experiment: Swap anti-aliased downsampling into one standard detector on one small-object-heavy dataset and compare size-stratified metrics against the unmodified twin.
main_risk: Modern learned downsampling may already approximate adequate low-pass behavior, leaving little to recover.
kill_risk: If small-object gains are indistinguishable from seed noise, the aliasing account of small-object failure is wrong.
community_default_belief: Small-object performance is limited by input resolution and feature-pyramid design, and is addressed by feeding larger images.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Resolution increases partially compensate for self-inflicted aliasing damage, so the field pays compute for a problem created by its own downsampling choices.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure recall of a frozen detector on the same small objects rendered at sub-pixel-shifted positions; strong shift-dependence of recall directly evidences aliasing sensitivity.

title: Objectness-guided zoom inference with scale-matched crop training
one_line_idea: Train on high-resolution crops whose object scales match the receptive-field sweet spot, then at inference use a cheap objectness prior to zoom only where needed.
problem: Full-image training forces one network to serve all scales simultaneously, wasting capacity, while uniform high-resolution inference wastes compute on empty regions; small objects lose on both ends.
core_hypothesis: Decoupling scale handling, with training on scale-normalized crops and inference through a low-cost zoom proposal stage, dominates uniform high-resolution processing on the accuracy-compute frontier for small-object workloads.
core_claim: A two-stage zoom pipeline with scale-matched crop training achieves equal or better small-object accuracy than uniform high-resolution inference at a fraction of the compute.
method_sketch: Train the detector on crops resampled so objects land in a narrow apparent-size band, train a lightweight full-image objectness heatmap network, and at inference process only heatmap-selected regions at high resolution with results merged.

kill_risk: If zoom-stage recall cannot exceed roughly the recall of cheap uniform processing, the pipeline is bounded by its own first stage and dies.
community_default_belief: The reliable route to small-object accuracy is training and testing at the highest affordable uniform resolution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniform resolution spends nearly all its compute on background, and the implicit assumption that proposals cannot be both cheap and high-recall is untested at modern backbone quality.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure recall of a tiny objectness network at generous overlap thresholds on small objects; if high recall is achievable cheaply, the pipeline premise stands.

title: Context versus pixels: factoring what small-object detection actually uses
one_line_idea: Quantify with swap experiments how much small-object detection relies on scene context versus object pixels, and exploit the answer with an explicit context-prior head.
problem: Below some apparent size, object pixels carry little discriminative information, and detectors probably rely on context, but the field does not know the size threshold where context becomes dominant nor design heads around it.
core_hypothesis: There exists a measurable size threshold below which context contributes more decision evidence than object pixels, and architecturally separating a context-prior pathway from an appearance pathway improves both accuracy and interpretability in that regime.
core_claim: Context-swap and pixel-scramble interventions will reveal a context-dominant regime, and a detector with an explicit scene-conditioned prior head will beat a monolithic baseline on sub-threshold objects.
method_sketch: Construct intervention sets by transplanting small objects into incongruent scenes and scrambling object interiors while preserving context, measure per-size accuracy under each intervention, then train a two-pathway head combining a scene-layout prior with local appearance.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy on tiny objects will drop far more under context replacement than under object-pixel scrambling, with the effect reversing above a characteristic apparent size.

why_possibly_novel: Context effects are documented qualitatively, but a quantitative size-resolved decomposition tied to an architectural consequence appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: A measured crossover size where context outweighs appearance evidence.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run context-swap and interior-scramble interventions on one dataset with one frozen detector and plot per-size accuracy degradation curves for both interventions.
main_risk: Generative editing artifacts in the interventions may confound the measurement of what evidence matters.
kill_risk: If no crossover exists and appearance dominates at every size, the two-pathway architecture has no justification.
community_default_belief: Detection evidence is local appearance, and context is a secondary cue that regularizes but does not carry decisions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At few-pixel scales local appearance is nearly uninformative, so decisions must already be context-driven, just invisibly inside the backbone.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Paste a small set of tiny objects into incongruent backgrounds and measure detection rate change with a frozen model in a day.

title: Density-adaptive query allocation for set-prediction detectors
one_line_idea: Let query-based detectors predict a spatial density map first and allocate decoder queries proportionally, instead of using a fixed query budget biased toward large salient objects.
problem: Set-prediction detectors use a fixed number of learned queries whose spatial coverage is trained to match average scenes, starving crowded regions of tiny objects while wasting queries on empty areas.
core_hypothesis: Query starvation, not feature quality, causes a measurable share of misses for small and dense objects in query-based architectures, and allocating queries from a predicted density map recovers those misses.
core_claim: A density-conditioned query generator improves recall on dense small-object regions at fixed total query count, outperforming simply increasing the number of fixed queries at matched compute.
method_sketch: Add a lightweight density head over encoder features, sample query reference points from the predicted density with a spatial spreading constraint, and train end to end with the standard matching loss plus a density supervision derived from ground-truth centers.
falsifiable_prediction: At equal query budgets, density-allocated queries will raise recall in the top decile of local object density substantially more than uniform or learned-static query placement.
why_important: Query-based detectors are becoming the default architecture, and their crowd behavior is a known practical weakness inherited by every downstream system.
why_possibly_novel: Dynamic and dense-prior queries have been explored in parts, but explicit density-proportional allocation with a starvation analysis at fixed budget appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat queries as a scarce resource to be spatially budgeted by predicted need.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a trained set-prediction detector to count unmatched ground-truth objects per local density bin, then retrain with density-allocated queries and re-measure the same accounting.
main_risk: End-to-end training with sampled query locations may be unstable or need gradient tricks that complicate the comparison.
kill_risk: If misses in dense regions persist with abundant nearby queries, starvation is the wrong diagnosis and the allocation cannot help.
community_default_belief: Increasing query count and improving matching stability are the accepted remedies for crowded-scene weakness in set-prediction detectors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: More uniform queries scale cost quadratically while still mismatching the spatial distribution of need, which is the actual constraint.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate per-region miss rate with distance to the nearest active query reference point in an existing model; a strong correlation validates starvation in hours.

title: Statistical instability of small-object average precision as a reporting hazard
one_line_idea: Quantify the sampling variance of size-stratified average precision and test the hypothesis that many reported small-object improvements are within resampling noise.
problem: Small-object average precision is computed from relatively few instances with high per-instance measurement noise, yet papers report gains without confidence intervals, so the community may be ranking methods on noise.
core_hypothesis: Bootstrap confidence intervals on small-object metrics for standard test sets are wide enough that typical reported inter-method gaps fall inside them, meaning much claimed progress in this regime is statistically unsupported.
core_claim: An instance-level bootstrap protocol plus seed-variance analysis will show that small-object metric noise is several times larger than for large objects, motivating mandatory intervals for size-stratified claims.
method_sketch: Implement image-level and instance-level bootstrap resampling of evaluation sets, train multiple seeds of representative detectors, decompose observed metric variance into data-sampling and training-stochasticity components, and publish a variance atlas per benchmark and size band.
falsifiable_prediction: The half-width of small-object metric confidence intervals will exceed commonly celebrated improvement margins, whereas large-object intervals will be comparatively tight.
why_important: If the effect is real, a chunk of the small-object literature ordering is unreliable, and cheap statistical hygiene would redirect effort toward real gains.

novelty_hook: Put error bars on the metric before trusting the leaderboard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap one standard test set for three public detectors and compare interval widths against the pairwise metric gaps among those detectors, stratified by object size.
main_risk: The conclusion may be dismissed as obvious while simultaneously being ignored in practice, limiting impact.
kill_risk: If intervals turn out narrow relative to typical gaps, the alleged reporting hazard does not exist and the project reduces to a confirmation of current practice.
community_default_belief: Point-estimate metric differences on established test sets are reliable evidence of method superiority at all size strata.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Variance scales inversely with effective instance count and small strata are exactly where counts collapse, a fact the uniform reporting convention ignores.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run instance-level bootstrap on one test set for one model pair and check whether their small-object gap exceeds the resampled interval, feasible in a day.

title: Detector-in-the-loop super-resolution restricted to proposal regions
one_line_idea: Train a super-resolution module with gradients flowing from the detection loss, applied only to candidate regions, instead of using perceptual super-resolution as a naive preprocessor.
problem: Off-the-shelf super-resolution optimizes perceptual quality, hallucinating textures that mislead detectors, while full-frame enhancement wastes compute; naive pipelines often fail to improve small-object accuracy.
core_hypothesis: Super-resolution optimized end to end for the detection objective on proposal regions learns task-relevant enhancement, improving small-object accuracy where perceptually trained enhancement does not.
core_claim: Region-restricted detection-supervised super-resolution beats both no-enhancement and perceptual super-resolution baselines on small-object metrics at moderate compute overhead.
method_sketch: Insert a compact enhancement network before second-stage feature extraction on candidate regions, train jointly with the detector loss without any perceptual objective, and compare against frozen perceptual enhancers in the same slot.
falsifiable_prediction: The task-supervised enhancer will improve small-object average precision over the no-enhancement control while the perceptual enhancer in the same architectural slot will not, isolating the objective as the causal factor.
why_important: It resolves a recurring practical dispute about whether super-resolution helps detection by showing the objective, not the enhancement concept, determines the answer.
why_possibly_novel: Task-driven super-resolution exists in scattered applications, but a controlled objective-isolation study in the proposal-restricted detection setting appears underexplored (novelty not verified).

minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the region enhancer under detection supervision and under frozen perceptual weights on one dataset, comparing size-stratified metrics of the two against no enhancement.
main_risk: Joint training may be dominated by detector adaptation to the enhancer rather than genuine information recovery, complicating interpretation.
kill_risk: If neither enhancer variant beats no-enhancement, the information simply is not recoverable and the direction is dead.
community_default_belief: Super-resolution is an image-quality tool whose benefits, if any, transfer to detection when plugged in as preprocessing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Perceptual objectives reward plausible texture, which is adversarial noise from the detector standpoint, so transfer should not be expected.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate a frozen detector on perceptually super-resolved versus raw small-object crops; if perceptual enhancement already helps consistently, the premise about its failure is wrong.

title: Center-plus-size-bin supervision as the honest label space for tiny objects
one_line_idea: For objects below the annotation noise floor, supervise center points with coarse size bins instead of full boxes, because precise extents are fiction at that scale.
problem: Tiny-object box edges are not reliably annotatable, yet training and evaluation pretend four precise coordinates exist, injecting noise into regression and rewarding overfitting to annotator habits.
core_hypothesis: Below a measurable size threshold, replacing box regression with center localization plus quantized size bins loses no task-relevant information while stabilizing training and improving downstream utility.
core_claim: A hybrid detector that switches label parameterization by apparent size will match or beat full-box training on human-validated small-object quality and downstream tracking initialization.
method_sketch: Determine the size threshold from inter-annotator box variance, train a detector whose head emits full boxes above threshold and center-plus-size-bin predictions below, and evaluate with center-distance metrics plus a downstream task where box precision allegedly matters.
falsifiable_prediction: The hybrid parameterization will improve center-localization accuracy for sub-threshold objects and will not degrade any downstream task that consumes the detections.
why_important: It aligns the label space with what humans can actually annotate, removing a systematic noise source from every small-object pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Point-based detection exists, but a size-conditional hybrid label space justified by measured annotator variance appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let measured annotability, not convention, choose the label parameterization per object.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one small-object dataset with some multi-annotator coverage, train hybrid versus full-box twins and compare center-error distributions and a downstream tracking or counting task.
main_risk: Downstream consumers may depend on box extents in unanticipated ways, making the coarse bins a hidden regression.
kill_risk: If full-box training matches the hybrid on center accuracy for tiny objects, the alleged harm from fictional edges is negligible.
community_default_belief: A detection is a box, and box quality should be maximized and measured at every object size uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: When inter-annotator edge variance approaches object size, the box abstraction stops encoding information and starts encoding noise.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute inter-annotator box agreement as a function of object size on an existing multi-annotated subset; if agreement stays high for tiny objects, the premise fails immediately.

title: Border-consistency training for tiled high-resolution inference
one_line_idea: Train detectors with an explicit tile-border consistency objective so the ubiquitous tiling trick stops systematically losing objects that straddle tile boundaries.
problem: High-resolution imagery is processed in overlapping tiles, and objects cut by tile borders suffer degraded detection and awkward merging heuristics, a failure mode that training never sees because training crops treat borders as image edges.
core_hypothesis: Simulating tiling during training, with a consistency loss tying predictions of the same object seen from adjacent tiles, removes most border-related misses without inference-time changes beyond standard overlap merging.
core_claim: Tile-consistency training improves recall for border-straddling objects substantially while leaving interior-object performance unchanged, and reduces sensitivity to the overlap-fraction hyperparameter.
method_sketch: During training, sample adjacent overlapping tile pairs, match predictions of shared-region objects across the pair, penalize score and box disagreement, and include truncated-object examples at synthetic borders with full-object supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall for objects within a border-width band of tile edges will approach interior recall after consistency training, whereas the control keeps a marked border deficit.

novelty_hook: Train for the tiling you will deploy, including its borders.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument border-band recall on one aerial dataset for a standard detector, retrain with tile-consistency sampling, and compare border-band versus interior recall.
main_risk: Gains may be achievable more simply by increasing tile overlap, making the training change unnecessary in compute-rich settings.
kill_risk: If border-band recall deficits are already negligible with standard overlap merging, the problem is imagined.
community_default_belief: Tiling artifacts are adequately handled by overlapping tiles and non-maximum suppression at merge time.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Merging fixes duplicates but cannot recover objects the per-tile detector never fired on due to truncation, which only training exposure can fix.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure per-object recall as a function of distance to tile border on an existing tiled pipeline; a visible dip validates the problem in hours.

title: Count-conditioned suppression to replace fixed non-maximum suppression in crowds
one_line_idea: Predict local object counts and condition the suppression stage on them, so crowded regions keep overlapping true positives that fixed-threshold suppression currently deletes.
problem: Non-maximum suppression assumes overlapping high-score boxes are duplicates, which is exactly wrong in crowds, and any fixed overlap threshold trades duplicate errors against deleted neighbors scene by scene.
core_hypothesis: A cheap local-count prediction carries enough information to modulate suppression aggressiveness spatially, dominating any fixed global threshold on the duplicate-versus-deletion tradeoff.
core_claim: Count-conditioned suppression improves crowded-region recall at matched duplicate rates compared with tuned fixed-threshold and learned-relation suppression baselines.
method_sketch: Add a density-map head trained from ground-truth centers, convert predicted local counts into per-region suppression budgets, and implement suppression that stops deleting once the regional survivor count matches the budget.
falsifiable_prediction: On dense pedestrian-style benchmarks the method will show strictly better recall-at-fixed-duplicate-rate curves in the densest quartile of regions than any fixed threshold of the same detector.
why_important: Crowd scenes are where detection failures have the highest human-safety stakes, and suppression is a known but under-attacked culprit.
why_possibly_novel: Learned and soft suppression variants exist, but budgeting survivors from an explicit predicted count field appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Suppression as a counting-constrained allocation problem rather than a pairwise-overlap heuristic.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the density head on one crowded dataset, apply budgeted suppression to frozen detector outputs, and compare duplicate-recall tradeoff curves against threshold sweeps.
main_risk: Count prediction may be unreliable at exactly the extreme densities where the method should help most.
kill_risk: If oracle ground-truth counts fed to the suppression stage do not improve the tradeoff, the framing itself is wrong regardless of count-head quality.
community_default_belief: End-to-end set-prediction architectures make suppression obsolete, so improving suppression is a dead end.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Widely deployed detectors still rely on suppression, and even set-prediction models exhibit duplicate-versus-deletion pathologies in crowds that a count prior could regulate.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Feed oracle local counts into budgeted suppression on existing detector outputs; if the tradeoff curve does not move, kill the idea same-day.

title: Density-adaptive matching relaxation for set-prediction training in crowds
one_line_idea: Relax one-to-one bipartite matching toward many-to-one as local ground-truth density rises, stabilizing set-prediction training exactly where matching flip-flops hurt most.
problem: One-to-one matching in set-prediction detectors becomes unstable in dense scenes because many near-equivalent assignments exist, producing noisy gradients and slow convergence precisely for crowded regions.
core_hypothesis: Matching instability, measurable as assignment churn across training iterations, concentrates in high-density regions and is causally linked to crowd performance, so density-conditioned relaxation of assignment uniqueness improves dense-scene accuracy.
core_claim: A matching scheme whose assignment multiplicity grows with local density reduces assignment churn and improves dense-region average precision over standard one-to-one and global one-to-many auxiliary schemes.
method_sketch: Log per-object assignment churn during baseline training to establish the correlation, then implement matching where each ground truth may claim up to k predictions with k a function of local neighbor count, annealing toward one-to-one late in training.
falsifiable_prediction: Assignment churn will correlate with local density, and the density-adaptive scheme will cut dense-region misses while matching baseline performance on sparse scenes.

why_possibly_novel: One-to-many auxiliary losses exist globally, but spatially density-conditioned multiplicity with churn-based diagnosis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let assignment multiplicity follow the local ambiguity it is meant to absorb.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument churn versus density on one crowded benchmark during baseline training, then train the adaptive variant and compare churn and density-stratified metrics.
main_risk: Relaxed matching may reintroduce duplicate predictions that the one-to-one design exists to prevent.
kill_risk: If churn shows no correlation with density, the diagnosis is wrong and the mechanism has no target.
community_default_belief: Matching instability is a global optimization nuisance addressed by auxiliary one-to-many heads and more queries, not a spatially structured phenomenon.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ambiguity that causes instability is inherently local geometry, so a global remedy misallocates relaxation to places that need none.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Parse assignment logs of an existing training run to correlate per-object matching churn with neighbor density; a scatter plot answers it in a day.

title: Cheap pairwise occlusion-order labels as crowd-detection supervision
one_line_idea: Collect binary who-is-in-front labels for overlapping instance pairs and use them to supervise an occlusion-reasoning head that disambiguates crowded detections.
problem: Crowded-scene errors concentrate on overlapping instances, but standard supervision gives no signal about occlusion structure, and full amodal or depth annotation is too expensive to collect at scale.
core_hypothesis: Pairwise occlusion-order labels, which are fast and reliable for humans to provide, carry enough structure to train an occlusion head whose features causally improve instance separation in crowds.
core_claim: Adding an occlusion-order prediction task on overlapping pairs improves crowded-region detection metrics beyond what the same annotation budget spent on more boxes achieves.
method_sketch: Annotate front-behind order for sampled overlapping ground-truth pairs, add a pairwise head predicting order from pooled joint features, train jointly with detection, and compare against a budget-matched control that spends the same annotation money on additional standard boxes.
falsifiable_prediction: The occlusion-supervised model will beat the budget-matched more-boxes control on dense-region recall and duplicate-related false positives.

why_possibly_novel: Occlusion reasoning exists in amodal segmentation, but budget-matched pairwise-order supervision for detection improvement appears underexplored (novelty not verified).

minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate order for a few thousand overlapping pairs on one crowded dataset, train with the auxiliary head versus the budget-matched control, and compare dense-region metrics.
main_risk: The auxiliary task may improve occlusion prediction without transferring to detection outputs.
kill_risk: If the more-boxes control matches or beats the occlusion-supervised model, the labels are not the best use of budget and the idea dies.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Boxes duplicate information the model already learns while occlusion order supplies a structurally missing signal, so marginal value per label can differ sharply.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Probe whether frozen detector features already predict occlusion order for overlapping pairs; high probe accuracy suggests the signal is redundant and the supervision unneeded.

title: Density as a covariate: stratified evaluation and density-conditioned normalization
one_line_idea: Treat local object density as an explicit covariate, reporting density-stratified metrics and conditioning detector normalization layers on estimated density.
problem: Detectors are trained and evaluated on density mixtures dominated by sparse scenes, so aggregate metrics hide nonlinear degradation with density and models internally miscalibrate activations in crowded inputs.
core_hypothesis: Detection performance degrades smoothly but nonlinearly with local density, and feature statistics shift with density in ways that density-conditioned normalization can correct cheaply.
core_claim: A density-stratified evaluation protocol reveals hidden failure curves across current detectors, and density-conditioned normalization recovers part of the high-density loss at negligible parameter cost.

main_risk: Density estimation errors at inference may inject their own noise into normalization, offsetting gains.
kill_risk: If activation statistics show no density dependence, the conditioning mechanism has nothing to correct.
community_default_belief: Detectors handle density variation implicitly, and crowded-scene weakness is an architecture problem rather than a distribution-conditioning problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Normalization layers bake in dataset-average statistics, and dense scenes are far from average, so a conditioning path may be the cheapest correction available.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Plot channel-mean drift of a frozen detector across density-binned inputs in one afternoon; visible drift justifies the mechanism.

title: Group-box representation for unsplittable object clusters
one_line_idea: Let detectors output group boxes with an estimated cardinality when instances cannot be reliably individuated, instead of forcing arbitrary instance splits that ground truth itself does not agree on.
problem: In dense clusters, even annotators disagree on how to split instances, yet detectors must commit to specific splits and are punished against one arbitrary ground-truth splitting, corrupting both training and evaluation.
core_hypothesis: Explicitly representing unsplittable clusters as group boxes with cardinality estimates matches the actual information content of the image and improves both counting accuracy and downstream usefulness compared with forced individuation.
core_claim: A detector with a group-output mode, evaluated under a protocol that accepts groups with correct extent and cardinality, yields more reliable counts and fewer spurious instance boundaries in dense imagery.
method_sketch: Identify low-agreement clusters via multi-annotator data or synthetic merging, train a head that chooses between instance and group outputs with a cardinality regressor, and define an evaluation that scores group extent plus count against clustered ground truth.
falsifiable_prediction: On dense clusters with documented annotator disagreement, group-mode outputs will achieve better count accuracy than forced instance splitting from the same backbone.
why_important: Counting and coverage, not exact individuation, are the actual downstream needs in many dense applications like inventory, biology, and crowd monitoring.
why_possibly_novel: Crowd-region annotations exist as ignore regions, but a first-class group-output representation with cardinality scoring appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Output the honest granularity: instance when possible, counted group when not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dense dataset subset with repeated annotation, compare count error of group-mode versus instance-mode outputs over low-agreement clusters.
main_risk: Downstream systems expecting per-instance outputs may not accept group outputs, limiting adoption regardless of accuracy.
kill_risk: If forced instance splitting already matches group-mode counting accuracy, the representation adds complexity without information gain.
community_default_belief: Detection means individuating every instance, and clusters should be handled with better instance separation methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: When the image genuinely lacks individuation evidence, demanding instances forces the model to fabricate boundaries, which is noise generation rather than detection.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure inter-annotator instance-count and split agreement in dense clusters of an existing dataset; low agreement establishes the representational gap immediately.

title: Instance-repulsion embeddings decoded into boxes for crowded scenes
one_line_idea: Learn per-pixel instance embeddings with explicit repulsion between neighboring objects, then decode boxes from embedding clusters, sidestepping box-space collisions in crowds.
problem: Crowded neighbors collide in box parameter space, confusing regression targets and suppression, whereas embedding spaces can keep arbitrarily close objects separable if trained with repulsion.
core_hypothesis: Moving instance disambiguation from box space to an embedding space with neighbor-repulsion losses reduces crowd-specific errors, because separation difficulty then scales with feature capacity instead of spatial overlap.
core_claim: An embed-then-decode detector will beat box-space baselines specifically on the high-overlap subset of crowded benchmarks while remaining competitive elsewhere.
method_sketch: Train per-pixel embeddings with pull-to-instance-center and push-from-neighbor terms, cluster embeddings at inference to form instances, fit boxes to clusters, and stratify evaluation by ground-truth pairwise overlap.
falsifiable_prediction: Errors on instance pairs with very high mutual overlap will drop markedly relative to box-regression baselines, with the advantage growing as overlap increases.
why_important: High-overlap pairs are where safety-relevant crowd failures live, and box-space methods have a structural ceiling there.
why_possibly_novel: Embedding-based instance separation is established in segmentation, but a detection-focused embed-then-decode pipeline evaluated on overlap-stratified crowds appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Disambiguate in a space where closeness is a choice, not a geometric fate.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the embedding head on a standard backbone for one crowded dataset and compare overlap-stratified detection metrics against the box-regression twin.
main_risk: Clustering at inference adds latency and failure modes that could erase theoretical separation advantages.
kill_risk: If embedding clusters merge exactly where boxes collide, the claimed decoupling of difficulty from overlap is false.
community_default_belief: Detection pipelines should predict boxes directly, and crowd problems are addressed within box space via better losses and suppression.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Box coordinates of heavily overlapping neighbors are nearly identical targets, an ill-conditioning that no box-space loss can fully remove but an embedding space dissolves by construction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train the embedding head briefly and visualize whether high-overlap ground-truth pairs remain separated in embedding space; visible merging kills it fast.

title: Weak count supervision as a regularizer for dense detection
one_line_idea: Use cheap region-level count labels to add a counting-consistency loss on detector outputs, recovering recall in dense regions without any extra boxes.
problem: Dense regions suffer systematic under-detection, and box annotation there is the most expensive of all, while approximate counts for a region are cheap to obtain yet unused by detection training.
core_hypothesis: A differentiable count-consistency penalty tying summed detection activations to region-level count labels pushes detectors to find objects they currently swallow in dense areas, improving recall beyond what the same budget in boxes yields.
core_claim: Count-supervised regularization improves dense-region recall at matched annotation budget compared with spending the budget on additional dense-region box labels.
method_sketch: Collect coarse counts for sampled dense regions, define a soft-count from detector output maps, penalize count mismatch alongside standard losses on the boxed subset, and evaluate against a budget-matched extra-boxes control.
falsifiable_prediction: The count-regularized model will reduce dense-region miss rate more per annotation-dollar than the extra-boxes control, with the advantage concentrated in the densest regions.
why_important: It opens a cheap, scalable supervision channel for the regime where standard supervision is least affordable.
why_possibly_novel: Counting and detection are usually separate tasks; count labels as a budget-efficient regularizer for detection recall appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Buy recall with counts, not boxes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one crowded dataset, simulate count labels from ground truth for a region sample, train with the consistency loss versus budget-matched extra boxes, and compare dense recall.
main_risk: The soft-count definition may be gameable, letting the model satisfy counts with diffuse activations rather than real detections.
kill_risk: If count consistency improves counts but not localized recall, the supervision does not transfer to the actual task.
community_default_belief: Detection recall improvements require instance-level localization supervision; aggregate labels are too weak to matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In dense regions the failure is systematic undercounting, exactly the error mode that even aggregate count constraints directly contradict.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Check whether current detector undercount in dense regions is large and systematic by comparing summed detections to ground-truth counts per region; a big consistent gap validates the target.
