title: Dense-region recall as a mandatory companion metric to mean average precision
one_line_idea: Introduce a standardized dense-region recall metric, because crowd-region ignore flags and instance averaging let mean average precision hide systematic dense-scene failures.
problem: Standard evaluation down-weights or ignores crowd regions and averages over instances, so a detector can post strong headline numbers while missing a large fraction of objects precisely where objects concentrate.
core_hypothesis: Current benchmark practice materially understates dense-region failure, and a recall metric computed over density-defined regions will reorder some methods relative to their headline metric ranking.
core_claim: A dense-region recall protocol, with density strata defined from ground truth and no crowd-ignore escapes, exposes performance differences invisible to standard metrics and correlates better with downstream crowd-task success.
method_sketch: Define density strata per image region, compute recall per stratum without ignore-region exemptions, publish an evaluation kit, and re-evaluate a set of public detectors to document ranking changes and correlation with a downstream counting task.
falsifiable_prediction: At least some pairs of public detectors will swap order between headline average precision and densest-stratum recall, demonstrating that the standard metric conceals the difference.
why_important: Metrics steer the field, and an evaluation blind spot in dense regions steers effort away from the highest-stakes failures.
why_possibly_novel: Density-aware analyses appear in individual papers, but a standardized no-exemption dense-recall companion metric with cross-model re-evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Remove the crowd-ignore escape hatch and see which methods were leaning on it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate several public detectors on one crowded benchmark with the stratified recall protocol and compare rankings against headline metrics.
main_risk: Ground-truth quality in the densest regions may be too poor to support a trustworthy recall computation.
kill_risk: If rankings never change and correlations with downstream tasks match the headline metric, the companion metric is redundant.
community_default_belief: Mean average precision with existing crowd handling is a sufficient summary of detector quality across scene types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging and exemptions are structurally biased against exposing concentrated failures, which is a property of the aggregation, not of the models.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute densest-stratum recall for two detectors with similar headline numbers; any large gap immediately demonstrates the blind spot.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Error decomposition showing tail classes fail at naming, then fixing naming with retrieval
one_line_idea: Decompose long-tail detection error into localization versus classification components, and if classification dominates, attach a nearest-exemplar retrieval head for tail classes.
problem: Long-tail detection methods mostly reweight losses without knowing whether rare classes fail because they are not localized or because they are misnamed, leaving the actual bottleneck unaddressed.
core_hypothesis: Rare classes are localized by class-agnostic machinery nearly as well as common classes but misclassified, so a retrieval-based naming head with a tail exemplar memory outperforms loss-reweighting approaches at equal cost.
core_claim: An oracle study will attribute most tail error to classification, and a k-nearest-exemplar head over frozen region features will recover a large fraction of oracle-classification headroom on tail classes.
method_sketch: Measure class-agnostic proposal recall and oracle-classification average precision per frequency bucket, then implement a memory of tail-class region embeddings with nearest-neighbor scoring blended into the classifier for rare classes only.
falsifiable_prediction: Tail-class proposal recall will be close to head-class recall, while the retrieval head will improve tail average precision substantially more than standard reweighting baselines at matched compute.
why_important: Correct bottleneck attribution redirects long-tail research and offers a practical path where new tail classes are added by inserting exemplars, not retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Retrieval-augmented classification exists, but a decomposition-driven justification with rare-class-only blending in detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Prove the bottleneck first, then patch precisely that component with memory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one long-tail benchmark, compute frequency-stratified proposal recall and oracle-classification metrics, then evaluate the retrieval head against a reweighting baseline.
main_risk: Region embeddings of rare classes may be too scattered for nearest-neighbor scoring to be reliable at very low shot counts.
kill_risk: If tail proposal recall turns out much lower than head recall, classification is not the bottleneck and the retrieval remedy is misdirected.
community_default_belief: Long-tail detection is primarily an imbalance problem to be fixed with sampling and loss reweighting during end-to-end training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reweighting redistributes gradient among classes but cannot inject the missing discriminative evidence that a few stored exemplars provide directly.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute class-agnostic proposal recall on tail classes for one trained detector; a high number confirms the naming-bottleneck premise within hours.

title: Calibrated coarse-fallback prediction for uncertain fine-grained detections
one_line_idea: Let detectors output a calibrated superclass label when fine-grained tail classification is uncertain, and define an evaluation that rewards correct-coarse over confidently-wrong-fine.
problem: Detectors are forced to emit leaf-level classes even when evidence only supports a coarser category, and current metrics score a reasonable coarse answer identically to a wild error, discarding usable information.
core_hypothesis: A hierarchical output policy with calibrated abstention to superclasses preserves downstream utility, and a hierarchy-aware metric will show that models differ substantially in coarse-fallback quality despite similar flat metrics.
core_claim: Hierarchy-aware prediction and scoring improves decision-usefulness of long-tail detections, measured by a downstream task where acting on a correct superclass is beneficial and acting on a wrong leaf is costly.
method_sketch: Attach a hierarchy from existing taxonomies, train or post-hoc-calibrate per-level confidences, emit the deepest level whose calibrated confidence clears a threshold, and evaluate with hierarchical scoring plus a simulated decision task with asymmetric costs.
falsifiable_prediction: Under asymmetric-cost evaluation, hierarchy-fallback outputs will dominate flat leaf-forced outputs for tail classes across a range of cost ratios.
why_important: Real consumers of detections almost always have usable coarse actions, and the flat-output convention throws away exactly the reliability tail classes lack.
why_possibly_novel: Hierarchical classification is old, but calibrated level-selection with cost-based detection evaluation for long-tail deployment appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Score detectors on knowing how much they know, level by level.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Post-hoc calibrate one detector per hierarchy level on a long-tail benchmark and compare flat versus fallback outputs under a defined cost matrix.
main_risk: Taxonomies may be arbitrary in places, making superclass fallback semantically unhelpful for some branches.
kill_risk: If per-level calibration is no better than leaf calibration, level selection has no informational basis.
community_default_belief: Detection outputs should be leaf-level classes, and hierarchical scoring is a niche complication rather than a deployment need.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tail-class evidence is often genuinely partial, and forcing leaf commitment converts partial knowledge into full errors that coarse outputs would avoid.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure how often the true superclass is top-ranked when the leaf prediction is wrong for tail classes; a high rate proves recoverable information exists.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Data value of curation versus collection for tail classes
one_line_idea: Run a controlled comparison of re-annotating and cleaning existing tail-class instances versus collecting new ones, measuring marginal metric gain per unit budget for each.
problem: Teams default to collecting more rare-class data, but existing tail annotations are disproportionately noisy and incomplete, and nobody has cleanly measured which budget allocation yields more detection improvement.
core_hypothesis: For many tail classes, fixing label errors and recovering missed instances in already-collected images produces more metric gain per budget unit than acquiring and annotating new images.
core_claim: A budget-matched experimental protocol will show curation dominating collection below a class-specific data-quality threshold, yielding a practical decision rule for long-tail data investment.
method_sketch: For a sample of tail classes, spend equal audited budgets on expert re-annotation of existing data versus new-image collection with standard annotation, retrain identical models per arm, and compare per-class metric gains with confidence intervals.
falsifiable_prediction: The curation arm will outperform the collection arm for classes whose measured initial annotation error exceeds a threshold, and underperform for clean classes, producing a crossing curve rather than a uniform winner.
why_important: Data budgets dominate practical detection costs, and an evidence-based allocation rule for the long tail would change how production datasets are grown.
why_possibly_novel: Data-centric studies exist for classification, but a budget-matched curation-versus-collection trial with per-class quality covariates in detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Measure the exchange rate between cleaning and collecting, per class.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick several tail classes on one benchmark, run both arms at small matched budgets, and compare per-class gains against measured initial annotation error rates.
main_risk: Results may be strongly dataset-specific, limiting the generality of the decision rule.
kill_risk: If collection uniformly dominates regardless of initial quality, the curation hypothesis is simply false.
community_default_belief: Rare-class performance problems are data-quantity problems, solved by getting more examples.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tail annotations suffer elevated error and missing-instance rates, so effective sample size is far below nominal, and cleaning raises it more cheaply than new collection.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Audit annotation error and missed-instance rates on a sample of tail-class images; if quality is already high, curation has no headroom and the study is unnecessary.

title: Semantic-similarity margins instead of frequency-based reweighting for the long tail
one_line_idea: Set per-class decision margins from each tail class's embedding similarity to confusable head classes, replacing frequency-derived weights that ignore what a class is actually confused with.
problem: Long-tail methods condition on class frequency alone, but a rare class's difficulty depends on which head classes crowd its decision region, something frequency statistics cannot see.
core_hypothesis: Tail-class errors concentrate on semantically adjacent head classes, and margins scaled by text-embedding or feature-space similarity to those neighbors outperform frequency-scaled margins at equal complexity.
core_claim: Similarity-aware margin assignment improves tail average precision over frequency-based baselines specifically by reducing tail-to-neighbor-head confusions, verifiable in the confusion structure.
method_sketch: Compute per-class neighbor similarity profiles from class-name embeddings and feature centroids, derive margin sizes that grow with neighbor proximity and inverse frequency jointly, train with a margin-based classification loss, and analyze confusion-matrix changes.
falsifiable_prediction: The gain over frequency-only margins will be concentrated in tail classes with close head neighbors, while isolated tail classes will show little difference, matching the mechanism.
why_important: It replaces a crude statistical prior with a structural one, plausibly unlocking tail gains that frequency reweighting has plateaued on.
why_possibly_novel: Margin-based long-tail losses exist, but margins driven by measured semantic neighborhood geometry rather than counts appear underexplored in detection (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Margin size should encode who your confusable neighbors are, not just how rare you are.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one detector with frequency margins and one with similarity-aware margins on a long-tail benchmark and compare tail metrics plus confusion flows toward neighbor head classes.
main_risk: Embedding similarity may misestimate visual confusability for classes whose names are semantically close but appearances distinct.
kill_risk: If tail errors are not concentrated on semantic neighbors in the baseline confusion matrix, the mechanism's premise is factually wrong for that data.
community_default_belief: Class frequency is the operative variable in long-tail learning, and per-class treatments should scale with rarity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two equally rare classes can differ enormously in difficulty depending on decision-region crowding, so frequency is a confounded proxy for the real variable.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Inspect a trained baseline's tail-class confusion matrix and measure what fraction of errors go to top-similarity head classes; a low fraction kills the premise quickly.

title: Context-compatible placement for copy-paste augmentation of rare classes
one_line_idea: Replace random copy-paste of tail-class instances with placement guided by scene-compatibility scoring, testing whether context violations are why naive pasting can hurt precision.
problem: Copy-paste augmentation boosts tail recall but pastes objects into implausible contexts, potentially teaching context-free features that inflate false positives for context-dependent classes.
core_hypothesis: The precision cost of copy-paste is driven by context violation, and placement guided by a scene-compatibility model retains the recall benefit while removing most of the precision loss.
core_claim: Compatibility-guided pasting outperforms random pasting on tail-class F-measure, with the difference concentrated in classes whose detection relies measurably on context.
method_sketch: Score candidate paste locations with a scene-layout compatibility model trained from natural co-occurrence statistics, paste tail instances only into compatible regions with plausible scale, and compare against random-paste and no-paste baselines with context-reliance measured per class.
falsifiable_prediction: For context-reliant classes, compatibility-guided pasting will preserve recall gains while significantly reducing the false-positive increase seen under random pasting.
why_important: Copy-paste is one of the cheapest long-tail tools available, and repairing its precision side effect would make it safely default-on.
why_possibly_novel: Context-aware augmentation has been touched on, but a mechanism-isolating comparison with per-class context-reliance covariates appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Diagnose the augmentation side effect and remove it, rather than discarding or blindly applying the augmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one long-tail benchmark, train with random versus compatibility-guided pasting at matched paste counts and compare per-class precision changes stratified by measured context reliance.
main_risk: The compatibility model may restrict placements so much that effective augmentation volume drops for exactly the rarest classes.
kill_risk: If random pasting shows no precision cost in careful measurement, the problem this solves is not real.
community_default_belief: Copy-paste is a broadly safe recall booster whose artifacts are minor relative to its benefits.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pasting decouples object from context, and for classes recognized partly through context this is a direct injection of misleading training signal.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare false-positive rates on context-mismatched validation scenes for models trained with and without random pasting; a visible gap validates the side effect immediately.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Memorization audit and near-duplicate control for tail-class evaluation
one_line_idea: Measure how much reported tail-class performance depends on near-duplicate or single-source instances shared across train and test, and publish a deduplicated tail evaluation.
problem: Tail classes often have few sources, so visually near-identical instances can appear in both training and evaluation, letting memorization masquerade as rare-class generalization.
core_hypothesis: A meaningful fraction of measured tail-class performance on standard benchmarks reflects near-duplicate leakage or single-scene redundancy, and controlling for it will materially lower and re-rank tail metrics.
core_claim: A perceptual-similarity audit of tail instances across splits, followed by leakage-controlled re-evaluation, will show inflated tail numbers and provide a cleaner protocol for future work.
method_sketch: Embed all tail-class instances, find cross-split near-duplicate pairs and same-scene clusters, quantify their contribution to per-class metrics, and release a deduplicated evaluation list plus re-scored baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class tail metrics will drop noticeably after leakage control for classes with high cross-split similarity, and some method rankings will change on the cleaned protocol.
why_important: If tail progress is partially leakage, the field is optimizing the wrong thing, and cleaned evaluation redirects effort toward genuine generalization.
why_possibly_novel: Duplicate audits exist for classification datasets, but a tail-focused cross-split leakage audit with re-ranked detection baselines appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Rare classes are where leakage hides best, because few sources exist and nobody has the instances memorized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run near-duplicate search between train and test tail instances on one benchmark and re-evaluate two public models with flagged instances removed.
main_risk: Perceptual similarity thresholds are debatable, and overly aggressive dedup could be accused of discarding legitimate test data.
kill_risk: If cross-split similarity is rare and metric changes are negligible, the leakage concern is unfounded for that benchmark.
community_default_belief: Standard dataset splits adequately separate train and test content, and tail metrics measure generalization to new instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Split protocols randomize images, not sources or scenes, and tail classes concentrate in few sources by definition of rarity.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Nearest-neighbor search from test tail instances into training data with a perceptual embedding; inspecting the top pairs by eye settles existence of leakage in a day.

title: Decoupling balanced feature learning from natural-prior score calibration
one_line_idea: Train detection features under balanced sampling but restore the natural class prior in a separate calibration stage, testing whether repeat-factor sampling's known head-class harm is a calibration artifact.
problem: Balanced sampling improves tail learning but distorts the effective class prior, miscalibrating head-class scores; current practice accepts this tradeoff instead of separating representation learning from prior correction.
core_hypothesis: The head-class cost of balanced sampling is mostly a score-prior distortion, recoverable by post-hoc prior correction, rather than a feature-quality degradation.
core_claim: Balanced-feature training plus natural-prior recalibration achieves tail gains without head losses, dominating both natural sampling and balanced sampling used alone.
method_sketch: Train with strong balancing, then fit a per-class score correction on a natural-distribution calibration split derived from the effective sampling prior, and compare the three regimes with per-frequency-bucket metrics and calibration errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Post-hoc prior correction will recover most of the head-class average precision lost to balanced sampling while retaining most tail gains, showing the tradeoff was largely an artifact.
why_important: It could dissolve a fundamental-seeming tradeoff in long-tail detection into a bookkeeping fix, changing default training recipes.
why_possibly_novel: Logit adjustment is known in classification; a systematic decoupling study in detection, where scores also gate suppression and matching, appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The imbalance tradeoff may live in the prior, not the features.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one long-tail benchmark, train natural, balanced, and balanced-plus-correction variants of the same detector and compare per-bucket metrics.
main_risk: Detection scores interact with suppression and matching nonlinearly, so classification-style prior correction may not transfer cleanly.
kill_risk: If head-class losses persist after ideal prior correction, balanced sampling genuinely harms features and the hypothesis is dead.
community_default_belief: Balanced sampling trades head performance for tail performance at the representation level, and the tradeoff must be tuned, not removed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sampling changes the implicit prior inside the score, and evaluating under the natural prior without correcting it confuses calibration error with representation error.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply analytic prior-ratio correction to the scores of an existing balanced-trained detector and re-evaluate; hours of work bounds how much is calibration.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Long-tail rarity as disguised annotation incompleteness
one_line_idea: Estimate per-class false-negative rates in ground truth and test whether a chunk of the long-tail problem is missing tail annotations penalizing correct detections as false positives.
problem: Tail classes are plausibly the most under-annotated, since annotators miss unfamiliar objects, so training punishes correct tail detections and evaluation undercounts them, compounding true rarity with measurement artifact.
core_hypothesis: Per-class annotation miss rates are systematically higher for tail classes, and correcting training and evaluation for estimated miss rates changes both absolute numbers and method rankings in long-tail detection.
core_claim: A miss-rate estimation protocol using cross-model consensus plus targeted human verification will document elevated tail miss rates and yield a corrected training loss that improves verified tail performance.
method_sketch: Flag high-confidence unmatched detections agreed by diverse models, verify a sample with humans to estimate per-class miss rates, then downweight negative loss on likely-missed regions and re-evaluate with verified-complete evaluation subsets.
falsifiable_prediction: Verified miss rates will be substantially higher for tail classes than head classes, and miss-rate-aware training will improve tail metrics on verification-completed evaluation data.
why_important: If rarity is partly artifact, the field's core benchmark numbers and the framing of long-tail research both need revision.
why_possibly_novel: Missing-annotation robustness is studied generically, but the specific coupling of miss-rate structure to class frequency with corrected benchmarking appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The tail may be quieter than it is small: unannotated, not absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate miss rates for a stratified class sample on one benchmark via consensus-plus-verification and test the frequency-missrate correlation.
main_risk: Consensus flagging inherits shared model biases, so miss-rate estimates need enough human verification to be credible, which costs money.
kill_risk: If miss rates show no relationship to class frequency, the disguise hypothesis is dead and standard rarity framing stands.
community_default_belief: Ground-truth completeness is roughly uniform across classes, and tail difficulty reflects true data scarcity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotator attention and recognition are frequency-biased human processes, so completeness should degrade exactly where classes are unfamiliar.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Human-verify a few hundred high-confidence unmatched tail-class detections from a strong model; the verified true-positive fraction estimates the miss rate directly.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Cross-dataset tail transplantation with domain harmonization
one_line_idea: Import tail-class instances from other datasets with explicit domain harmonization, and measure whether class rarity or domain gap is the binding constraint on transfer.
problem: Tail classes in one dataset are often well represented in another, but naive cross-dataset mixing underperforms, and the field lacks a controlled account of whether domain shift or label-convention mismatch causes the failure.
core_hypothesis: Domain and convention gaps, not intrinsic uselessness of foreign examples, block cross-dataset tail transfer, so harmonizing low-level statistics and box conventions unlocks most of the foreign data's value.
core_claim: A transplantation pipeline with appearance harmonization and annotation-convention mapping will recover a large share of the gain achievable by in-domain tail data of equal quantity.
method_sketch: Select tail classes with foreign coverage, harmonize color and noise statistics plus box-tightness conventions toward the target dataset, mix with weighting, and compare against in-domain-data upper bounds and naive-mixing baselines at matched instance counts.
falsifiable_prediction: Harmonized transplantation will close well over half of the naive-mixing-to-in-domain gap for most transplanted classes, with residuals correlated with measured domain distance.
why_important: The world's detection datasets jointly cover most tails, and a working transfer recipe converts fragmented labels into shared capability.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-dataset training is common, but tail-targeted transplantation with convention harmonization and a rarity-versus-domain decomposition appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat other datasets as tail-class organ donors with explicit compatibility matching.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a handful of classes present in two public datasets, compare naive mixing, harmonized mixing, and in-domain-equivalent controls on the target benchmark.
main_risk: Class-definition mismatches across datasets may be semantic rather than stylistic, unfixable by any statistical harmonization.
kill_risk: If harmonization yields no improvement over naive mixing, the domain-gap diagnosis is wrong and transfer failure is semantic.
community_default_belief: Cross-dataset detection data mixes poorly, and per-dataset collection remains necessary for tail classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mixing failures may be dominated by fixable low-level and convention mismatches that no one bothered to correct class-specifically.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fine-tune with naive versus histogram-and-convention harmonized foreign tail data for two classes and compare per-class metrics in a couple of GPU-days.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Per-class operating thresholds as a first-class output of long-tail detection
one_line_idea: Learn and ship per-class decision thresholds from small calibration sets, and evaluate detectors by deployed per-class operating performance instead of threshold-free ranking metrics.
problem: Deployments use one global confidence threshold, but under class imbalance the optimal threshold varies wildly by class, so tail classes are silently gated out and the ranking-based benchmark metric never reveals it.
core_hypothesis: The gap between global-threshold and per-class-threshold operating performance is large, dominated by tail classes, and per-class thresholds estimated from very few labeled examples per class transfer reliably.
core_claim: A threshold-learning procedure with per-class small-sample calibration and hierarchical shrinkage yields deployed F-measure far above global thresholds, and reporting this operating gap should become standard.
method_sketch: Estimate per-class score distributions with shrinkage toward class-group priors from limited calibration data, derive thresholds per target precision, and evaluate deployed-operating metrics across calibration-set sizes against global-threshold baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class thresholds from even tens of examples per class will beat the best single global threshold by a wide margin on tail-class F-measure without hurting head classes.
why_important: It addresses the deployment step everyone performs and nobody benchmarks, likely worth more in practice than many architectural gains.
why_possibly_novel: Threshold selection is folk practice; a shrinkage-based small-sample protocol with an operating-gap reporting standard for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Benchmark the thresholding step itself, since users deploy thresholds, not precision-recall curves.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one long-tail benchmark, compare deployed F-measure under global versus shrinkage-estimated per-class thresholds across calibration budgets.
main_risk: Score distributions may drift between calibration and deployment data, eroding small-sample threshold validity.
kill_risk: If a well-tuned global threshold comes within noise of per-class thresholds, the operating gap is negligible and the protocol is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Threshold-free metrics like average precision capture what matters, and thresholding is a trivial deployment detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ranking quality and operating quality diverge under imbalance, and the divergence lands precisely on the classes long-tail research claims to care about.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Sweep a global threshold versus oracle per-class thresholds on existing model outputs; the gap computes from cached predictions in hours.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Unknown-not-negative treatment of unmatched confident predictions
one_line_idea: Treat confident detector predictions that match no ground truth as unknown rather than negative during training, using estimated annotation miss rates to set the treatment.
problem: Standard training assumes ground truth is complete, so every unmatched prediction is punished as a false positive, but real datasets miss instances and the punishment teaches the detector to unlearn true detections.
core_hypothesis: Excluding or downweighting the negative loss on high-confidence unmatched predictions, gated by an estimated per-class miss rate, improves recall without the precision collapse that naive ignore-all policies cause.
core_claim: A miss-rate-gated unknown treatment strictly dominates both the standard complete-annotation assumption and blanket ignore policies on datasets with documented annotation incompleteness.
method_sketch: Estimate per-class miss rates from cross-model consensus with small human verification, define an unknown zone in score space whose width scales with the miss rate, exclude unknown-zone unmatched predictions from the negative loss, and evaluate on verification-completed test data.
falsifiable_prediction: On incompleteness-verified benchmarks, the gated treatment will improve recall at matched precision, with gains proportional to the measured per-class miss rate.
why_important: Annotation incompleteness is ubiquitous and grows with dataset scale and vocabulary size, making complete-annotation training assumptions increasingly wrong.
why_possibly_novel: Ignore-region and sparse-annotation methods exist, but coupling the unknown zone width to empirically estimated per-class miss rates appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Calibrate how much to distrust the ground truth, class by class, and train accordingly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one dataset with a verification-completed subset, train standard, blanket-ignore, and gated variants and compare recall-precision on the completed subset.
main_risk: Miss-rate estimates may be biased by shared model blind spots, mis-sizing the unknown zone.
kill_risk: If gains never exceed the blanket-ignore baseline, the per-class gating adds no information and the idea reduces to prior art.
community_default_belief: Ground truth is treated as complete, and unmatched predictions are false positives by definition during training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Measured annotation completeness in large datasets is materially below one hundred percent, so the definitional assumption is empirically false in a structured, correctable way.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Human-verify a sample of high-confidence unmatched predictions from a strong model on one dataset; the true-positive fraction directly quantifies the mislabeled-negative problem.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Latent annotator-style modeling for box tightness harmonization
one_line_idea: Model annotator identity as a latent variable that shifts box tightness, learn per-annotator offsets, and predict boxes in a harmonized canonical style.
problem: Different annotators and guidelines produce systematically different box tightness, so models learn an average of inconsistent styles and transfer poorly across datasets with different conventions.
core_hypothesis: Box tightness style is a low-dimensional, learnable per-annotator or per-dataset factor, and factoring it out during training yields sharper localization and better cross-dataset transfer.
core_claim: A detector trained with latent style variables and style-marginalized inference outperforms standard training on cross-dataset localization metrics and reduces within-dataset regression variance.
method_sketch: Where annotator identifiers or dataset sources exist, learn per-source affine box corrections jointly with detection; where they do not, infer latent style clusters via expectation-maximization over residual patterns; output canonical-style boxes at inference.
falsifiable_prediction: Style-factored training will improve localization when evaluated against consensus boxes and show clearly better box-quality transfer to datasets with different tightness conventions.
why_important: Cross-dataset and cross-vendor training is the norm in industry, and unmodeled convention mismatch is a persistent silent quality drain.
why_possibly_novel: Annotator modeling exists in classification crowdsourcing, but latent tightness-style factorization for box regression appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Boxes have accents; learn them and translate to a canonical dialect.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with annotator identifiers or on a merged multi-source corpus, train with and without style factors and compare localization against small consensus-annotated subsets.
main_risk: Style may interact with object class and size in ways a low-dimensional factor cannot capture.
kill_risk: If residual analysis shows no annotator-consistent tightness structure, there is no style to factor out.
community_default_belief: Box annotation noise is unstructured jitter best handled by robust losses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human annotators are consistent within themselves and different from each other, which is structured bias, not jitter, and robust losses cannot exploit structure they ignore.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Group regression residuals of a trained model by annotator or source and test for significant mean differences; a day of analysis on existing data.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Structured confusion-aware noise adaptation for detection class labels
one_line_idea: Estimate the class-confusion structure of annotation errors and train detectors through a noise-adaptation layer built from that structure, instead of assuming uniform label noise.
problem: Class label errors in detection datasets are concentrated on confusable pairs, but noise-robust training methods largely assume unstructured noise, wasting the strong prior that errors follow semantic similarity.
core_hypothesis: A confusion-structured noise model, estimated from repeated annotations or model-annotator disagreement patterns, enables a transition-matrix-style correction that improves fine-grained detection accuracy over uniform-noise-robust baselines.
core_claim: Confusion-aware noise adaptation recovers accuracy on confusable class pairs that both standard training and uniform-noise methods lose, verifiable through corrected confusion matrices on cleanly re-annotated evaluation subsets.
method_sketch: Estimate a sparse class-confusion transition matrix from multi-annotation samples, attach a differentiable noise layer applying the transition during training so the base classifier learns clean posteriors, and evaluate on expert-re-annotated subsets.
falsifiable_prediction: Gains over uniform-noise baselines will concentrate on class pairs with high estimated confusion mass, matching the structural mechanism.
why_important: Fine-grained vocabularies keep growing and confusable-pair noise grows with them, making structured noise handling steadily more valuable.
why_possibly_novel: Transition-matrix methods are established in classification, but structured estimation and adaptation for detection, where matching noise compounds class noise, appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Label noise has a semantic shape; train through the shape, not around it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate the confusion structure on one fine-grained detection dataset from a doubly annotated sample, train with and without the noise layer, and compare on expert-verified evaluation.
main_risk: Estimating the transition matrix for many classes from limited repeated annotation may be underdetermined.
kill_risk: If annotation errors turn out to be mostly localization or missing-instance errors rather than class swaps, the class-noise layer targets a minor error mode.
community_default_belief: Label noise in detection is a minor issue handled implicitly by large data volume and robust training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Volume averages out unstructured noise but systematically consistent confusions bias the learned decision boundaries no matter the scale.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Audit a sample of repeated annotations to measure what fraction of label disagreements are semantic swaps between confusable pairs; the fraction sizes the opportunity immediately.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Error-type drift tracking in teacher-student detection self-training
one_line_idea: Track the composition of pseudo-label error types across teacher-student generations and inject targeted disagreement regularization to stop specific error modes from amplifying.
problem: Semi-supervised detection amplifies whatever systematic biases the teacher has, but pipelines monitor only aggregate metrics, so specific error modes like small-object suppression can grow generation over generation unnoticed.
core_hypothesis: Pseudo-label error composition drifts predictably across self-training rounds, with confidence-filtered pipelines progressively suppressing hard true positives, and a per-error-type monitoring plus targeted correction loop prevents the drift cheaply.
core_claim: An error-taxonomy tracker over self-training rounds will document directional drift, and reweighting pseudo-label acceptance per error-prone stratum will yield better final models than uniform confidence thresholds.
method_sketch: Classify pseudo-label errors against held-out ground truth into taxonomy bins per round, plot compositional drift, then adapt per-stratum acceptance thresholds and compare final-model metrics against uniform-threshold self-training.
falsifiable_prediction: Confidence-thresholded self-training will show growing under-representation of small and occluded objects in pseudo-labels across rounds, and stratified acceptance will reduce the final small-object performance gap.
why_important: Self-training is the workhorse of industrial detection data engines, and unmonitored drift silently shapes what deployed models can see.
why_possibly_novel: Confirmation bias in self-training is known abstractly, but a quantitative error-composition drift analysis with stratified acceptance correction for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Monitor what kind of wrong the loop amplifies, not just how wrong.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run three self-training rounds on one dataset, log pseudo-label error composition per round, and compare uniform versus stratified acceptance variants.
main_risk: Error taxonomies require held-out labels to compute, which may not represent the unlabeled pool where drift actually happens.
kill_risk: If error composition is stable across rounds, drift is a non-problem and stratified acceptance is unnecessary complexity.
community_default_belief: A single confidence threshold with strong augmentation suffices to keep pseudo-label quality adequate across self-training rounds.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence is systematically lower for exactly the object strata that are hardest, so uniform thresholds are a biased filter whose bias compounds through the loop.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare the size and occlusion distribution of accepted pseudo-labels against ground truth after one round; a visible skew evidences the filtering bias in one experiment.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Shape-aware aggregation of crowdsourced boxes beyond coordinate averaging
one_line_idea: Replace coordinate-wise averaging of multi-annotator boxes with shape-aware aggregation that models annotator error structure, especially for elongated and occluded objects.
problem: Crowdsourcing pipelines average multiple annotators' boxes coordinate-wise, but for elongated, diagonal, or partially occluded objects the average of plausible boxes can be a box no annotator would draw and worse than the best individual.
core_hypothesis: Annotator box errors are structured by object geometry and occlusion, and an aggregation model accounting for this structure produces consensus boxes closer to expert reference than averaging or majority-style heuristics.
core_claim: Shape-aware aggregation measurably improves consensus-label quality on difficult geometry subsets, and detectors trained on the better consensus labels inherit the improvement.
method_sketch: Collect or reuse multi-annotator box data with expert adjudication on a subset, fit an aggregation model with per-annotator reliability and geometry-conditioned error terms, and compare downstream detector quality trained on each aggregation's outputs.
falsifiable_prediction: On elongated and occluded object subsets, shape-aware consensus will be closer to expert boxes than coordinate averaging, and the training-label improvement will propagate to detector localization metrics.
why_important: Aggregation is a universal, invisible stage of dataset construction whose errors permanently contaminate everything trained downstream.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation aggregation theory is developed for categorical labels, but geometry-conditioned box aggregation with downstream detection validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The consensus box is a statistical estimator; design it, do not default to the mean.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-annotated subset with expert reference, compare aggregation methods by expert-distance on geometry-stratified objects, then retrain one detector per label set.
main_risk: Gains may be confined to a small subset of difficult geometries, diluting downstream impact.
kill_risk: If coordinate averaging is within noise of expert boxes across geometries, the estimator design space is already saturated.
community_default_belief: Averaging several annotators' boxes reliably yields labels better than any single annotator.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging assumes unimodal symmetric error, but occlusion and ambiguous extent create multimodal annotation distributions where the mean falls between modes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On existing multi-annotator data, find objects where annotator boxes form clusters and check whether the mean box lands off-cluster; counting such cases takes a day.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Annotator disagreement maps as difficulty supervision for detection training
one_line_idea: Use per-instance annotator disagreement as an auxiliary signal that predicts where models will fail, weighting training and flagging evaluation accordingly.
problem: Multi-annotator disagreement is collected and then discarded by aggregation, though it plausibly marks exactly the ambiguous instances where model errors and metric noise concentrate.
core_hypothesis: Instance-level annotator disagreement correlates strongly with model error, and using disagreement as a soft difficulty weight during training plus an ambiguity flag during evaluation improves both learning and measurement.
core_claim: Disagreement-weighted training improves performance on unambiguous instances without sacrificing ambiguous ones, and disagreement-stratified evaluation shows that a sizable share of inter-model metric differences comes from ambiguous instances where ground truth is unstable.
method_sketch: Quantify disagreement per instance from existing multi-annotator data, train with disagreement-modulated loss weights, and stratify evaluation into agreement tiers to re-examine model comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: Model errors will concentrate on high-disagreement instances, and inter-model ranking on the high-agreement tier will differ from the aggregate ranking for some model pairs.
why_important: It recycles an already-paid-for annotation byproduct into both a training signal and a measurement hygiene tool.
why_possibly_novel: Disagreement modeling is common in subjective-label tasks, but systematic reuse for detection difficulty weighting and evaluation stratification appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Disagreement is data, not waste from consensus building.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-annotated detection dataset, correlate instance disagreement with a public model's errors and re-rank two models on agreement-stratified evaluation.
main_risk: Most large datasets lack per-instance multi-annotation, limiting where the method applies without new collection.
kill_risk: If disagreement and model error are weakly correlated, the signal carries no usable difficulty information.
community_default_belief: Aggregated consensus labels are sufficient and annotator disagreement is noise to be eliminated in dataset construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Disagreement encodes genuine ambiguity in the image-label relation, which is informative about both learnability and metric reliability.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the error rate of one frozen detector on high versus low disagreement instances of an existing multi-annotated subset; a same-day correlation check.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Ground-truth-noise-adjusted metric intervals for detection benchmarks
one_line_idea: Report detection metrics as intervals reflecting estimated ground-truth noise, so benchmark differences are interpreted against label uncertainty instead of treated as exact.
problem: Benchmarks report point metrics against imperfect ground truth, and once model quality approaches label quality, metric differences may reflect noise-fitting rather than genuine capability, with no standard way to see this.
core_hypothesis: Propagating estimated annotation error rates through the metric computation yields uncertainty intervals wide enough to change conclusions in some published-style comparisons, particularly for high-performing models on mature benchmarks.
core_claim: A noise-propagation evaluation kit, parameterized by measured miss, class-swap, and box-jitter rates, produces defensible metric intervals and identifies which strata of a benchmark still discriminate between strong models.
method_sketch: Estimate the three noise-rate types from multi-annotation or verification samples, propagate via perturbation resampling of the ground truth through the metric pipeline, and publish per-benchmark discriminability maps by size, class, and density strata.
falsifiable_prediction: For strong recent detectors on mature benchmarks, metric intervals under realistic noise parameters will overlap for some model pairs whose point metrics differ by typical claimed margins.
why_important: It provides the field a principled stopping criterion for benchmark chasing and a map of where measurable progress remains possible.
why_possibly_novel: Label-noise impact studies exist piecemeal, but a general noise-propagation interval kit for detection metrics with discriminability maps appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Metrics with error bars inherited from the labels themselves.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate noise rates on one benchmark from existing repeated annotations, resample perturbed ground truths, and compute metric interval widths for two strong public models.
main_risk: Noise-rate estimates themselves carry uncertainty, and adversarial choices could make intervals arbitrarily wide, requiring conservative, documented parameterization.
kill_risk: If realistic noise parameters produce negligible interval widths, ground-truth noise does not threaten current benchmark conclusions and the kit is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Benchmark ground truth is accurate enough that metric point differences of typical reported size reflect real model differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: As models close in on the label noise floor, an increasing share of the remaining metric variance is annotation artifact, invisible without propagation analysis.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Perturb ground truth with plausible jitter and miss rates on one validation set and measure how much a strong model's metric moves; one day bounds the sensitivity.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Track-consistency mining of annotation errors in video-derived detection datasets
one_line_idea: Exploit temporal consistency in the source videos of frame-sampled detection datasets to automatically flag missing, spurious, and misclassified annotations.
problem: Many detection datasets are sampled from video, but their annotations are audited frame-independently, ignoring that an object present in adjacent frames but unlabeled in the middle one is almost surely an annotation miss.
core_hypothesis: Temporal interpolation and tracking through source video identifies annotation errors with high precision, enabling cheap dataset repair that measurably improves models trained on the repaired labels.
core_claim: A track-consistency audit will flag errors at high verified precision, and retraining on repaired annotations will improve performance on independently verified evaluation data.
method_sketch: Recover or approximate source-video continuity, run tracking across annotated frames, flag inconsistencies between tracks and per-frame labels, verify a flagged sample with humans to measure precision, and retrain on repaired labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Human verification will confirm the majority of flagged inconsistencies as genuine annotation errors, and repaired-label training will yield measurable metric gains on clean evaluation.
why_important: It offers near-free label quality improvement for the large family of video-derived datasets, attacking noise at the source rather than in the loss function.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal consistency is used for pseudo-labeling, but as a systematic annotation-audit and repair tool with verified precision on existing benchmarks it appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The dataset's own temporal structure is an unused error detector.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one video-derived dataset with accessible source clips, run the audit on a subset, human-verify a few hundred flags, and report flag precision by error type.
main_risk: Source videos may be unavailable or frame provenance unrecoverable for the most popular datasets.
kill_risk: If flag precision is low, the audit generates review burden rather than repairs and the approach fails.
community_default_belief: Dataset annotations are audited by sampling and spot checks, and per-frame independence of labels is an acceptable simplification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal coherence is a strong physical prior that frame-independent auditing throws away, leaving a large class of detectable errors undetected.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Manually inspect temporal label consistency for a few dozen tracks in one video-derived dataset; the observed inconsistency rate immediately sizes the opportunity.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Cross-split perceptual leakage audit for detection benchmarks
one_line_idea: Systematically audit detection benchmarks for near-duplicate images and scenes across train-test splits and quantify how much leakage inflates reported performance.
problem: Detection benchmarks were assembled from web sources and video with limited duplicate control, and no standardized audit quantifies how near-duplicate leakage across splits affects reported detection metrics.
core_hypothesis: Perceptual near-duplicates and same-scene pairs exist across splits in standard detection benchmarks at non-trivial rates, and their removal measurably reduces metrics for models trained on the full data, with larger effects for higher-capacity models.
core_claim: A public leakage audit with embedding-based duplicate detection and human verification will produce cleaned evaluation lists on which some inter-model gaps shrink, quantifying the memorization share of benchmark performance.
method_sketch: Embed all images with a self-supervised model, mine cross-split nearest neighbors, human-verify a stratified sample to set duplicate thresholds, publish cleaned test lists, and re-score public models on cleaned versus original evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Metric drops on cleaned evaluation will be small but systematic and will correlate with model capacity, and a handful of benchmark comparisons will change materially.
why_important: Trustworthy benchmarks are the field's measurement infrastructure, and detection has escaped the leakage scrutiny applied elsewhere.
why_possibly_novel: Duplicate audits were influential in classification; an equivalent systematic audit with re-scored detection baselines appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Do for detection benchmarks what duplicate audits did for classification ones.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine and verify cross-split near-duplicates on one benchmark and re-evaluate two public detectors on the cleaned list.
main_risk: The leakage rate may be low enough that the audit's main finding is reassurance, which is publishable service work but not a discovery.
kill_risk: If verified leakage is negligible and metric changes are within noise, the inflation hypothesis is dead for that benchmark.
community_default_belief: Established detection benchmark splits are clean enough that leakage is not a factor in reported results.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web-scraped and video-derived collections naturally contain near-duplicates, and split protocols randomized at image level cannot control scene-level redundancy.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run nearest-neighbor search from a random test sample into the training split with a perceptual embedding and eyeball the top pairs; existence and rough rate of leakage is a one-day check.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Forced-choice soft labels for genuinely ambiguous class boundaries
one_line_idea: For instances where annotators genuinely disagree between two classes, store a two-class soft label from forced-choice statistics instead of resolving to a single class, and train detectors on the soft target.
problem: Dataset pipelines force ambiguous instances like van-versus-truck into single classes, injecting boundary noise that miscalibrates detectors precisely on the class pairs where deployment confusion matters most.
core_hypothesis: Preserving ambiguity as a soft label over the disputed pair improves calibration and cross-pair discrimination compared with majority-resolved hard labels, at negligible annotation cost when disagreement statistics already exist.
core_claim: Soft-label training on ambiguous pairs yields better calibrated pairwise posteriors and equal or better hard accuracy, with the improvement visible in deployment-style threshold transfer between the confusable classes.
method_sketch: Identify high-disagreement instance sets from annotation logs, encode empirical annotator distributions as soft targets for those instances only, train with mixed hard-soft supervision, and evaluate pairwise calibration and accuracy on expert-adjudicated instances.
falsifiable_prediction: On expert-adjudicated evaluation of confusable pairs, soft-trained models will show lower calibration error and fewer high-confidence wrong predictions than hard-label twins.
why_important: High-confidence confusions between adjacent classes are among the most operationally damaging detection errors, and this attacks their supervision-side cause.
why_possibly_novel: Soft labels are standard as regularization, but empirically grounded pairwise ambiguity encoding from annotation logs in detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Keep the ambiguity the pipeline currently destroys; it is signal about the world.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one dataset with annotation logs, train hard versus mixed-soft twins and compare pairwise calibration on adjudicated confusable instances.
main_risk: Annotation logs with per-instance disagreement may be unavailable for most public datasets, requiring some new collection.
kill_risk: If hard-label training with modern regularization already achieves equal pairwise calibration, the preserved ambiguity adds nothing.
community_default_belief: Every instance has one correct class, and annotation pipelines should resolve disagreements before training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some category boundaries are genuinely graded in the world, so the single-class assumption is a modeling error, not an annotation problem.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Check whether a model trained on majority labels is overconfident on known-ambiguous instances by comparing its entropy there versus on clean instances; an immediate calibration diagnostic.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Deployment-aligned metric suite exposing what mean average precision hides
one_line_idea: Standardize a companion metric suite of fixed-false-positive-rate recall, calibration error, and threshold-transfer robustness, because mean average precision is provably insensitive to properties deployments depend on.
problem: Mean average precision evaluates score rankings, so two detectors with identical rankings but wildly different calibration, score stability, and operating-point behavior receive identical scores while behaving very differently in production.
core_hypothesis: Detectors with similar mean average precision differ substantially on deployment-relevant axes, and these differences predict production incident rates better than the headline metric.
core_claim: A standardized deployment-metric suite will reveal large hidden variance among detectors matched on headline metrics and will correlate better with task-level outcomes in downstream case studies.
method_sketch: Define the suite precisely, evaluate a broad set of public detectors matched on headline metrics, quantify hidden variance, and validate against downstream task outcomes such as tracking quality and alert precision in simulated deployments.
falsifiable_prediction: Among detectors within a small headline-metric band, deployment-suite scores will spread widely and will rank models consistently with downstream task success where the headline metric cannot distinguish them.
why_important: The gap between benchmark and deployment behavior is a chronic industry complaint, and metric infrastructure is the cheapest place to fix it.
why_possibly_novel: Each component metric exists somewhere, but a standardized suite with cross-model hidden-variance quantification and downstream validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Measure the properties deployments consume, not just the ranking researchers optimize.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several public detectors with similar headline numbers on the suite and on one downstream task, testing whether suite scores predict task outcomes.
main_risk: Downstream validation is task-specific, and critics can always dispute the chosen tasks' representativeness.
kill_risk: If suite scores track headline metrics almost perfectly across models, the hidden variance does not exist and the suite is redundant.
community_default_belief: Mean average precision is an adequate single-number summary for comparing detectors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ranking quality is invariant to monotone score transforms while deployments are not, so the metric is blind by construction to an entire equivalence class of behavioral differences.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute calibration error and fixed-false-positive recall for two similarly ranked public detectors; any large spread on cached outputs demonstrates the blindness within hours.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Standardized regime-decomposed reporting of detection performance
one_line_idea: Make size-by-density-by-frequency decomposed metric reporting a standard machine-readable artifact, so regime-specific regressions stop hiding inside aggregate improvements.
problem: Papers report aggregate metrics, and a method that improves large sparse common objects while regressing small dense rare ones shows a net gain, silently steering the field away from hard regimes.
core_hypothesis: A substantial fraction of recent method-over-baseline improvements are regime-nonuniform, with hidden regressions in small, dense, or rare strata that aggregate metrics mask.
core_claim: A standardized decomposition artifact and a re-analysis of public model pairs will document the prevalence of hidden regime regressions and enable regression-aware method comparison.
method_sketch: Define a canonical strata grid over size, local density, and class frequency, build an evaluation tool emitting per-cell metrics with uncertainty, re-analyze many public checkpoint pairs, and report the frequency and magnitude of masked regressions.
falsifiable_prediction: A meaningful percentage of method-versus-baseline comparisons will contain at least one stratum with a statistically supported regression despite aggregate improvement.
why_important: Aggregate-only reporting is a field-steering mechanism, and cheap tooling can realign incentives toward uniform progress.
why_possibly_novel: Per-size numbers exist informally, but a canonical multi-axis decomposition with uncertainty and a prevalence study of masked regressions appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Audit progress for regime uniformity, not just direction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the decomposition on a handful of public detector pairs from method papers and count strata with supported regressions.
main_risk: Fine strata have few instances, so uncertainty handling must be careful to avoid crying regression on noise.
kill_risk: If masked regressions turn out rare across many pairs, aggregate reporting is vindicated and the artifact is merely convenient.
community_default_belief: An aggregate metric improvement means the method is better, with per-stratum behavior a secondary detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregates weight strata by instance counts that mismatch deployment importance, so net gains can coexist with harm in the strata practitioners care about most.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Decompose one celebrated method-baseline pair by size and density; a single clear hidden regression proves the phenomenon exists.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Global-ranking average precision to test cross-class score comparability
one_line_idea: Introduce a metric that ranks all detections across classes in one list, because per-class average precision never tests the cross-class score comparability that global-threshold deployments rely on.
problem: Mean average precision computes rankings within each class and then averages, so a detector whose scores are incomparable across classes loses nothing on the benchmark but fails badly under the single global threshold most deployments use.
core_hypothesis: Detectors differ substantially in cross-class score comparability, and a global-ranking metric will expose these differences and correlate with global-threshold deployment performance where mean average precision does not.
core_claim: Global-ranking average precision, reported alongside the standard metric, will reorder some public models and predict single-threshold operating quality across classes.
method_sketch: Pool all detections across classes into a single ranked list against all ground truths, compute the global-ranking metric, evaluate public detectors, and correlate the gap between global and per-class metrics with measured cross-class calibration divergence.
falsifiable_prediction: Models with similar standard metrics will show visibly different global-ranking scores, and the difference will track cross-class score-distribution divergence.
why_important: The metric-deployment mismatch it targets affects nearly every practical detection system that uses one threshold for many classes.
why_possibly_novel: Class-agnostic evaluations exist in fragments, but a deliberate cross-class-comparability metric with deployment-correlation validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Test the scores where deployments actually use them: in one shared ranking.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute global-ranking and standard metrics for several public detectors from cached outputs and compare orderings plus per-class score-distribution alignment.
main_risk: Global ranking mixes class difficulty with calibration, requiring careful analysis to attribute differences correctly.
kill_risk: If global and per-class metrics rank all tested models identically, cross-class incomparability is not a practical differentiator.
community_default_belief: Averaging per-class average precision fairly summarizes multi-class detection quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The per-class construction structurally exempts the score comparability property that single-threshold deployment makes load-bearing.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Overlay per-class score distributions of correct detections for one detector; visible cross-class misalignment on cached outputs takes an afternoon and validates the concern.

title: Adjudicated top-loss auditing to measure benchmark annotation ceilings
one_line_idea: Human-adjudicate the highest-loss predictions of strong detectors on mature benchmarks to measure what fraction of remaining model error is actually ground-truth error.
problem: As detectors improve, an unknown share of their residual benchmark error is annotation mistakes rather than model mistakes, so continued optimization may be fitting label noise while the field cannot tell.
core_hypothesis: For strong models on mature detection benchmarks, a large minority or majority of top-loss disagreements will adjudicate in the model's favor, implying current headline numbers understate model quality and overstate remaining headroom.
core_claim: An adjudication protocol over stratified top-loss samples will quantify the annotation ceiling per benchmark and produce corrected headroom estimates that change how progress should be read.
method_sketch: Sample top-loss false positives and false negatives per stratum for two or three strong public models, adjudicate with multiple experts and clear guidelines, estimate the ground-truth-error share with uncertainty, and extrapolate corrected metric ceilings.
falsifiable_prediction: The adjudicated ground-truth-error share among top-loss items will be substantial for mature benchmarks and concentrated in small objects, crowds, and ambiguous classes.
why_important: Whether the field's flagship numbers are near a label-noise ceiling determines the value of further benchmark chasing versus new evaluation construction.
why_possibly_novel: Spot fixes of test labels have happened, but a stratified, uncertainty-quantified ceiling estimate from top-loss adjudication for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Measure how much of the remaining error is the benchmark's fault, not the model's.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Adjudicate a few hundred stratified top-loss disagreements for one strong model on one benchmark and report the ground-truth-error fraction with intervals.
main_risk: Adjudicator disagreement on genuinely ambiguous items may leave a wide uncertainty band on the ceiling estimate.
kill_risk: If adjudication overwhelmingly sides with the ground truth, the ceiling is far away and the premise of exhausted benchmarks fails.
community_default_belief: Residual benchmark error of strong detectors represents real capability gaps worth optimizing away.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotation error rates that were negligible against weak models become the dominant error term against strong ones, without anyone changing the labels.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One expert reviews one hundred top-loss items of a strong public model; even this rough pass estimates the annotation-error share within a day.

title: Verified-dispute evaluation for open-vocabulary detection under incomplete ground truth
one_line_idea: Add a human-verification stage for disputed false positives in open-vocabulary evaluation, because incomplete ground truth systematically penalizes exactly the detectors that find more real objects.
problem: Open-vocabulary test sets cannot exhaustively annotate all valid objects for arbitrary vocabularies, so better detectors surface more unannotated true objects and are scored as worse, an evaluation bias that grows with detector quality.
core_hypothesis: A protocol that routes a stratified sample of unmatched confident detections to human verification and corrects metrics accordingly will materially change open-vocabulary rankings, favoring models currently punished for their recall.
core_claim: Verified-dispute evaluation produces corrected metrics with quantified uncertainty at modest verification cost, and some model comparisons will flip relative to raw incomplete-ground-truth scoring.
method_sketch: Define dispute sampling stratified by score and class, collect human verdicts with quality control, correct precision estimates via the verified sample with statistical extrapolation, and publish the protocol plus corrected leaderboard deltas for public models.
falsifiable_prediction: The verified true-positive fraction among disputes will be substantial and model-dependent, and at least some model pairs will change order after correction.
why_important: Without dispute correction, open-vocabulary evaluation actively selects against the property it exists to measure.
why_possibly_novel: Incomplete-annotation biases are acknowledged, but an operational verification-and-correction protocol with corrected rankings appears underexplored for open-vocabulary detection (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let models appeal their false positives, with humans as the court.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two public open-vocabulary detectors on one benchmark, verify a few hundred stratified disputes each and compute corrected precision deltas.
main_risk: Verification cost scales with vocabulary breadth, and sampling design must be careful to keep extrapolation honest.
kill_risk: If dispute verification finds mostly genuine false positives across models, ground-truth incompleteness is not distorting rankings and the protocol is unneeded.
community_default_belief: Unmatched detections are false positives, and incomplete annotation is uniform noise that affects all models equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Incompleteness penalizes models proportionally to how many missing-but-real objects they find, which is precisely non-uniform across model quality.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Human-check one hundred top-score unmatched detections from a strong open-vocabulary model; the verified-real fraction measures the bias directly in a day.

title: Compute-normalized comparison to separate method gains from resolution gains
one_line_idea: Require accuracy-per-compute frontier reporting for detection methods, testing the hypothesis that many claimed small-object improvements are repackaged resolution and test-time compute increases.
problem: Detection papers compare methods at unequal inference compute, and since resolution strongly drives small-object accuracy, method-versus-compute confounding may explain a chunk of reported architectural progress.
core_hypothesis: When representative recent methods are re-evaluated along matched compute-resolution frontiers, a substantial portion of their claimed advantages over baselines will shrink, particularly in small-object strata.
core_claim: A frontier-based comparison protocol and a re-analysis of public methods will quantify the confounded share of recent progress and establish compute-honest reporting as a community norm.
method_sketch: Re-evaluate public method-baseline pairs across resolution and test-time-augmentation sweeps, fit accuracy-compute frontiers per method, compare frontier separations instead of point comparisons, and stratify by object size.
falsifiable_prediction: For several prominent pairs, frontier separation will be much smaller than reported point gaps, and for some pairs the frontiers will cross or coincide within uncertainty.
why_important: Compute-confounded comparisons misallocate research attention and industry adoption decisions on a large scale.
why_possibly_novel: Compute-aware reporting is urged generically, but a systematic frontier re-analysis of detection method claims with size stratification appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Compare frontiers, not points, or the resolution knob does the talking.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick two public method-baseline pairs, sweep resolution for each, and compare frontier gaps against the published point gaps.
main_risk: Reproducing published configurations faithfully enough for fair frontiers is laborious and contestable.
kill_risk: If frontier gaps match point gaps across tested pairs, the confounding concern is empirically minor.
community_default_belief: Published method comparisons at chosen operating points fairly represent methodological progress.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Operating points are chosen by authors optimizing headline numbers, and resolution-compute settings are a free variable that correlates suspiciously with claimed gains.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one baseline at the higher resolution used by the method it was compared against; if the gap collapses, confounding is demonstrated in one experiment.
