title: Counterfactual object-edit unit tests for detection robustness
one_line_idea: Build a suite of controlled generative edits, removing, occluding, recoloring, and relocating objects, and score detectors on correct sensitivity and invariance, properties aggregate metrics never test.
problem: Standard evaluation measures correlation with annotations on natural images, so it cannot distinguish a detector that uses object evidence from one exploiting context and dataset regularities, and it never verifies causal responsiveness to object presence.
core_hypothesis: Detectors matched on benchmark metrics will diverge widely on counterfactual tests, revealing shortcut reliance, and counterfactual scores will predict robustness under natural distribution shift better than the headline metric.
core_claim: A generative-edit test suite with verified edit quality provides a causal behavioral fingerprint of detectors that adds independent, deployment-relevant information to standard metrics.
method_sketch: Use inpainting and compositing pipelines with human quality filtering to create edit sets, define pass criteria per edit type, evaluate public detectors, and correlate suite scores with performance on independent shifted-distribution benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Suite scores will spread widely among benchmark-matched detectors and will rank-correlate with shifted-distribution performance where the headline metric does not.
why_important: Causal behavior verification is standard practice in software engineering and absent in detection evaluation, despite deployment failures that are exactly causal misbehaviors.
why_possibly_novel: Perturbation robustness suites exist for corruption noise, but object-level counterfactual behavioral testing with shift-prediction validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Unit tests for detectors: remove the object, the box must disappear.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create a few hundred verified removal and occlusion edits on one dataset, evaluate three public detectors, and check score spread plus correlation with an existing shift benchmark.
main_risk: Generative artifacts could contaminate the tests, requiring careful filtering to ensure edits, not artifacts, drive detector responses.
kill_risk: If all benchmark-matched detectors pass or fail the suite identically, the fingerprint adds no discriminative information.
community_default_belief: High benchmark accuracy implies detectors have learned to rely on genuine object evidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correlational evaluation cannot detect shortcut strategies that exploit stable dataset regularities, which only interventions can expose.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Remove objects via inpainting on fifty images and check whether a strong detector still fires at the vacated locations; persistent firing evidences shortcut reliance within a day.

title: Mandatory resampling intervals for detection benchmark claims
one_line_idea: Establish instance-level bootstrap and seed-variance intervals as required reporting for detection benchmarks, and empirically test how many typical method gaps clear the resulting significance bar.
problem: Detection papers claim superiority from single-run point differences, but nobody has systematically measured whether typical claimed margins exceed the joint noise of test-set sampling and training stochasticity.
core_hypothesis: The combined interval from evaluation resampling and multi-seed training is wide enough that a nontrivial fraction of typical published-scale margins would not clear it, especially in small-object and rare-class strata.
core_claim: A cheap standardized interval protocol plus an empirical study of margin-versus-noise across representative model pairs will quantify the reliability crisis, if any, and give the community an adoptable reporting bar.
method_sketch: Implement paired bootstrap over images and instances, train multiple seeds for representative architectures to measure training variance, combine into interval recipes, and audit a sample of recent method-baseline gaps against the intervals.
falsifiable_prediction: Training-plus-sampling intervals will exceed a meaningful fraction of surveyed margins in at least the small-object and tail-class strata, while headline aggregate margins will more often clear the bar.
why_important: If the ordering signal the community optimizes against is partly noise, cheap statistical hygiene beats most modeling work in expected value.
why_possibly_novel: Variance concerns are raised sporadically, but a combined-noise audit with an adoptable interval recipe for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Price the noise before buying the improvement.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two architectures, train several seeds each, bootstrap the test set, and compare the combined interval to their published-scale gap in aggregate and per stratum.
main_risk: Multi-seed training cost limits how many architectures the study can cover, inviting sampling criticism.
kill_risk: If typical margins comfortably exceed combined intervals everywhere, current practice is vindicated and the protocol is merely optional hygiene.
community_default_belief: Standard test sets are large enough that single-run point differences of typical size are trustworthy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Effective sample sizes collapse in exactly the strata where methods claim their advantages, and training stochasticity adds a variance term no one measures.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Retrain one baseline with three seeds and measure the spread of its small-object metric; if seed spread rivals typical claimed gaps, the concern is validated immediately.

title: Automated false-positive taxonomy profiling as a standard evaluation artifact
one_line_idea: Automatically classify every false positive into a behavioral taxonomy, background texture, object part, similar class, duplicate, or context hallucination, and report the profile alongside aggregate metrics.
problem: Two detectors with equal false-positive counts can have completely different error characters with different deployment consequences, but current metrics compress this into one number and hide the difference.
core_hypothesis: False-positive profiles are stable model fingerprints that differ systematically across architectures and training recipes, and profile shape predicts deployment-specific failure costs better than the count alone.
core_claim: An automated, validated taxonomy classifier for detection false positives will reveal architecture-correlated error signatures and enable cost-weighted model selection that aggregate metrics get wrong.
method_sketch: Define taxonomy rules using ground-truth geometry, class similarity, and duplicate structure, validate the automatic classifier against human labels on a sample, profile many public detectors, and demonstrate cost-weighted selection scenarios where profiles reverse aggregate-based choices.
falsifiable_prediction: Distinct architecture families will show reproducibly different false-positive profiles at matched aggregate rates, and cost-weighted rankings will diverge from aggregate rankings for realistic cost matrices.
why_important: Error character determines deployment harm, and making it visible turns model selection from folklore into measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Error-analysis tooling exists for offline diagnosis, but a standardized automated profile as a reported artifact with cross-model signature analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Report what kind of wrong, not just how much wrong.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the classifier, validate on a human-labeled sample, and profile five public detectors to test signature stability and ranking divergence under cost weighting.
main_risk: Taxonomy boundary cases may make automatic classification noisy enough to blur genuine signatures.
kill_risk: If profiles are statistically indistinguishable across model families, false-positive character is not a model property and profiling adds nothing.
community_default_belief: False positives are homogeneous errors adequately summarized by precision at a given recall.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different inductive biases plausibly produce different hallucination modes, a structure the scalar summary is blind to by construction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Manually categorize one hundred false positives each from two different-architecture detectors; a visible profile difference validates the fingerprint claim in a day.

title: Operating-point regret as the metric for threshold transfer under shift
one_line_idea: Measure how much performance a validation-tuned threshold loses on shifted test conditions, defining operating-point regret as a first-class robustness metric for detection.
problem: Robustness evaluations report accuracy under shift at oracle-optimal thresholds, but deployed systems carry thresholds tuned on clean validation data, and the extra loss from stale thresholds is never measured.
core_hypothesis: Threshold-transfer regret is a large, model-dependent component of real-world robustness that is poorly correlated with oracle-threshold shifted accuracy, meaning current robustness rankings mispredict deployed behavior.
core_claim: An operating-point-regret protocol will show that some models with worse oracle-shifted accuracy are actually better deployed under shift because their score distributions are more stable, reordering robustness leaderboards.
method_sketch: For public detectors and standard shift suites, tune thresholds on clean validation, evaluate on shifts at both stale and oracle thresholds, define regret as the gap, and analyze which training choices minimize regret.
falsifiable_prediction: Regret will vary widely across models at matched oracle-shifted accuracy, and rankings by deployed performance will differ from rankings by oracle-shifted accuracy for some pairs.
why_important: It measures the robustness quantity deployments actually experience, likely explaining part of the persistent benchmark-production gap.
why_possibly_novel: Score-drift under shift is known qualitatively, but regret as a standardized metric with cross-model analysis for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Robustness of the operating point, not just of the ranking.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three public detectors on one corruption suite at stale versus oracle thresholds and compare regret spread against oracle-accuracy spread.
main_risk: Regret depends on the threshold-tuning recipe, requiring a canonical recipe to keep comparisons fair.
kill_risk: If regret is uniformly small or perfectly correlated with oracle-shifted accuracy, the new metric adds no information.
community_default_belief: Shifted-accuracy at fixed evaluation protocols captures what matters about detection robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shift moves score distributions as well as accuracy, and only the former determines what a frozen threshold delivers in production.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute clean-tuned versus oracle thresholds for one detector on one corruption type from cached outputs; the regret number falls out in hours.

title: Label assignment as a latent variable learned by expectation-maximization
one_line_idea: Treat which predictions are responsible for which ground truths as a latent variable optimized jointly with the network, unifying hand-crafted assignment heuristics under one learnable objective.
problem: Detection training depends on label assignment rules chosen by hand, and each generation of heuristics implicitly encodes untested priors about which spatial evidence should own each object.
core_hypothesis: Assignment heuristics are approximations to the expectation step of a latent-assignment likelihood, and optimizing that likelihood directly adapts assignment per dataset regime, beating any fixed heuristic across diverse regimes simultaneously.
core_claim: An expectation-maximization formulation of assignment, with soft responsibilities updated from current model likelihoods, matches specialized heuristics in their home regimes and beats them off-regime without retuning.
method_sketch: Define a per-object likelihood over candidate predictions, alternate soft responsibility updates with gradient steps, anneal responsibility entropy over training, and evaluate one recipe across sparse, dense, small-object, and long-tail datasets against tuned heuristic baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: The learned-assignment model will show smaller cross-dataset variance in performance than every fixed heuristic, while matching the best heuristic within each dataset.
why_important: It would replace a fragile, expertise-heavy component of every detector with a principled, self-tuning mechanism.
why_possibly_novel: Individual adaptive assignment schemes exist, but an explicit latent-variable formulation evaluated for cross-regime robustness of one recipe appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Assignment heuristics are frozen E-steps; unfreeze them.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the expectation-maximization assignment on one standard detector and compare against two heuristic baselines on one sparse and one dense dataset with identical schedules.
main_risk: Joint optimization of responsibilities and weights may find degenerate assignments early in training that stall learning.
kill_risk: If per-dataset tuned heuristics beat the learned assignment everywhere, the latent formulation adds cost without benefit.
community_default_belief: Label assignment is an engineering choice per architecture and dataset, converging on community-standard heuristics that work well enough.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Each heuristic hard-codes regime assumptions, and the regime diversity of real deployments guarantees some mismatch that a learned mechanism could absorb.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare two standard heuristics across a sparse and a dense dataset; if their ranking flips between regimes, no fixed heuristic is universally right and the learned approach has a target.

title: Rank-consistency training to align classification scores with localization quality
one_line_idea: Add a training loss that enforces agreement between score ranking and localization quality ranking among candidate boxes for the same object, attacking the misalignment where the highest-score box is not the best box.
problem: Detectors frequently rank a worse-localized box above a better one for the same object, so suppression keeps the wrong candidate and evaluation counts an avoidable localization error, a misalignment standard losses do not directly penalize.
core_hypothesis: Score-quality misalignment is a measurable, causally harmful phenomenon, and a pairwise rank-consistency loss over same-object candidates reduces it, converting existing localization capacity into realized metric gains without new features.
core_claim: Rank-consistency training improves final metrics at fixed backbone quality by ensuring the box that survives suppression is the best available one, with gains proportional to the baseline's measured misalignment.
method_sketch: During training, identify candidate sets per ground truth, add a pairwise loss penalizing score inversions relative to localization-quality order, and evaluate misalignment statistics plus standard metrics against controls including existing quality-estimation heads.
falsifiable_prediction: The frequency of best-box-not-top-score events will drop substantially, and average precision at strict localization thresholds will improve more than at loose thresholds.
why_important: It harvests performance the model already possesses but throws away at the ranking step, which is cheaper than adding capacity.
why_possibly_novel: Quality-estimation heads exist, but directly supervising the ranking consistency among same-object candidates appears underexplored as the primary objective (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The best box often already exists; teach the score to find it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure best-box inversion rates on a trained baseline, retrain with the pairwise loss, and compare inversion rates and strict-threshold metrics.
main_risk: Localization-quality targets are computed against noisy ground truth, so the consistency loss partly fits annotation jitter.
kill_risk: If baseline inversion rates are already low, there is little misalignment to harvest and gains cannot exist.
community_default_belief: Classification confidence is an adequate proxy for detection quality, with quality heads offering marginal refinements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Classification and localization objectives are trained with weak coupling, so their agreement is incidental rather than enforced, leaving systematic inversions.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one trained detector, count how often the top-scored candidate for an object has visibly lower overlap than another candidate; cached outputs answer this in hours.

title: Differentiable suppression-aware training to close the train-test pipeline gap
one_line_idea: Train detectors through a differentiable relaxation of the suppression stage so the loss matches what evaluation actually measures after duplicate removal.
problem: Training losses score raw predictions while evaluation scores post-suppression survivors, so models optimize an objective that differs from the measured one, leaving duplicate-related and ranking errors invisible to the loss.
core_hypothesis: A soft, differentiable suppression layer during training aligns the optimization target with post-suppression reality, reducing duplicate false positives and suppression-induced misses without inference-time changes.
core_claim: Suppression-aware training improves final metrics, with the improvement concentrated in crowded regions where suppression decisions are most consequential.
method_sketch: Implement a soft suppression operator with temperature-controlled overlap penalties, compute the task loss on post-suppression soft survivors, anneal toward hard suppression across training, and keep standard inference.
falsifiable_prediction: Duplicate false positives and crowd-region misses will both decrease relative to a standard-loss twin, and gains will grow with scene density.
why_important: It removes a structural objective mismatch present in most deployed detection pipelines at zero inference cost.
why_possibly_novel: End-to-end suppression alternatives exist, but a drop-in differentiable-suppression training loss for standard pipelines with density-stratified validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Optimize what the benchmark measures: the survivors, not the candidates.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrain one standard detector with the soft-suppression loss and compare density-stratified metrics and duplicate statistics against its twin.
main_risk: The soft relaxation may differ enough from hard suppression that training optimizes a third objective matching neither.
kill_risk: If gains vanish when the annealing reaches hard suppression, the relaxation was doing regularization, not alignment, and the theory fails.
community_default_belief: Suppression is a fixed post-processing step, and training on raw predictions with good assignment approximates the deployed objective well enough.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mapping from raw predictions to survivors is nonsmooth and interaction-heavy in crowds, exactly where the approximation breaks worst.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Quantify the loss-metric mismatch by measuring how often training-loss improvements fail to move post-suppression validation metrics across checkpoints; existing logs may already answer it.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Measuring and scheduling around gradient conflict between detection heads
one_line_idea: Quantify gradient conflict between classification and localization heads across training and apply conflict-aware update surgery only when and where conflict is measured, not uniformly.
problem: Multi-task interference between detection heads is assumed and treated with static loss weights, but nobody has mapped when during training, where in the network, and for which object strata the gradients actually conflict.
core_hypothesis: Head gradient conflict is structured, concentrating in specific layers, training phases, and object strata such as small objects, and targeted conflict resolution outperforms both static weighting and uniform gradient-surgery methods.
core_claim: A conflict atlas across layers, time, and strata will reveal exploitable structure, and phase-and-layer-targeted surgery will beat uniform application at equal compute.
method_sketch: Instrument per-layer cosine conflict between head gradients throughout training, stratify by object size and density of the batch content, then activate projection-based surgery only in measured conflict zones and compare against uniform and no-surgery controls.
falsifiable_prediction: Conflict will be phase- and layer-localized rather than uniform, and targeted surgery will match or beat uniform surgery while modifying far fewer updates.
why_important: It converts folklore about detection multi-task interference into a measured map with a cheaper, more effective intervention.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient surgery is generic multi-task machinery; a detection-specific conflict cartography driving selective application appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Map the interference before medicating it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument conflict on one detector training run, identify hot zones, and run targeted versus uniform surgery comparisons on the same recipe.
main_risk: Conflict metrics based on gradient cosine may not capture the interference that actually harms final performance.
kill_risk: If conflict is uniformly low or uncorrelated with stratum performance, the interference narrative itself is wrong for modern detectors.
community_default_belief: Detection heads coexist adequately under tuned static loss weights, and multi-task interference is a solved nuisance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Static weights cannot be right across all phases and strata simultaneously if conflict is nonstationary, which no one has checked at detection-relevant granularity.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Log per-layer head-gradient cosines for a few epochs of an existing recipe; the presence or absence of structured conflict is visible within days.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Annotation-agreement curriculum for detection training
one_line_idea: Schedule training from high-agreement to low-agreement instances using annotation-model consensus as the difficulty signal, testing when hard, ambiguous examples help versus poison detection training.
problem: Detection training treats all instances as equally trustworthy targets from the start, though ambiguous and noisy instances plausibly destabilize early representation formation while being necessary later for boundary refinement.
core_hypothesis: Instance difficulty measured by annotator-model agreement identifies examples whose early inclusion harms learning, and an agreement-based curriculum improves final performance over uniform and anti-curriculum orderings.
core_claim: A curriculum deferring low-agreement instances to late training beats uniform sampling on final metrics, and the benefit correlates with the dataset's measured noise level.
method_sketch: Score instances by consensus among annotations and an ensemble of weak models, define curricula from the score, train identical detectors under uniform, curriculum, and anti-curriculum orderings on datasets with different noise profiles, and compare final metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: Curriculum ordering will help on noisy datasets and be neutral on clean ones, while anti-curriculum will hurt noisiest datasets most, tracing the mechanism to noise rather than difficulty per se.
why_important: Data ordering is a free hyperparameter at scale, and a validated ordering rule would transfer across the entire detection training ecosystem.
why_possibly_novel: Curricula exist broadly, but agreement-derived difficulty with noise-stratified validation in detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Order by label trustworthiness, not by loss magnitude.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one noisy and one clean dataset, run the three orderings with identical budgets and compare final metrics with seed replication.
main_risk: Agreement scores conflate ambiguity, noise, and genuine difficulty, potentially deferring exactly the hard-but-clean examples that drive learning.
kill_risk: If ordering effects are within seed noise on all datasets, instance ordering is immaterial at detection scale and the direction dies.
community_default_belief: Uniform random sampling over the dataset is near-optimal, and curricula matter little for detection at practical scales.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniform sampling was validated mostly on relatively clean benchmarks, and industrial detection data is far noisier, where early noise exposure plausibly matters.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train briefly with the noisiest decile excluded versus included on one noisy dataset; an early-metric gap justifies the full curriculum study.

territory: Object detection: open-vocabulary, small/dense objects, long-tail classes, label noise, detection-specific training and evaluation gaps
title: Size-conditioned box parameterization mixtures
one_line_idea: Let the detector select among box parameterizations, center-size, corners, distance-to-edges, per object as a function of apparent size, because each parameterization has a size-dependent error profile.
problem: Detectors commit to one box parameterization globally, but regression error structure differs by parameterization and object size, so any single choice is suboptimal somewhere in the size range.
core_hypothesis: Parameterization-specific error profiles vary systematically with object size, and a size-conditioned mixture or gating of parameterizations reduces localization error across the full range simultaneously.
core_claim: A mixture head with size-dependent gating over three standard parameterizations improves size-stratified localization over each single-parameterization twin at negligible parameter cost.
method_sketch: Train single-parameterization twins to document size-error profiles, then train a gated mixture head whose gate takes predicted size, decode via the selected or blended parameterization, and evaluate size-stratified localization quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Single parameterizations will show crossing error-versus-size curves, and the mixture will track the lower envelope of those curves within noise.
why_important: Localization quality at strict thresholds is a persistent gap, and a free-lunch improvement from representation choice would apply to nearly every architecture.

fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate size-stratified localization for two existing public models differing mainly in parameterization; visible profile differences justify the controlled study.

title: Universal objectness pretraining from motion and depth cues
one_line_idea: Pretrain a class-agnostic objectness backbone at scale from unlabeled video motion and depth discontinuities, then attach classifiers with minimal box supervision, testing whether localization is learnable without any human boxes.
problem: Every detector relearns objectness from human boxes, yet motion boundaries and depth discontinuities in unlabeled video plausibly carry most of the objectness signal for free, leaving human boxes needed only for naming.
core_hypothesis: Objectness pretrained from physical cues transfers across categories and domains, cutting the box-label requirement for a target detection task by a large factor at matched performance.
core_claim: A physics-cue-pretrained objectness backbone will reach target-task parity with standard pretraining using several times fewer labeled boxes, with the advantage largest for novel domains.
method_sketch: Mine motion segments and depth edges from unlabeled video with classical and self-supervised estimators, pretrain a proposal backbone to predict these cues, then fine-tune detectors with varying labeled-box budgets and compare label-efficiency curves against standard initialization.
falsifiable_prediction: The label-efficiency curve of the cue-pretrained backbone will lie strictly above the standard curve in the low-label regime, with parity requiring several-fold fewer boxes.
why_important: Box annotation is the dominant cost in detection deployment, and a label-efficiency multiplier from free video would restructure data budgets everywhere.
why_possibly_novel: Motion-based objectness has a long history, but scaled cue pretraining evaluated by label-efficiency multiples on modern architectures appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Physics teaches where things are; humans only need to teach what they are called.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain on a moderate unlabeled video corpus, fine-tune on one benchmark at three label budgets, and compare against identically budgeted standard-pretrained twins.
main_risk: Static-scene objects without motion or depth contrast may be underrepresented in the pretraining signal, biasing objectness coverage.
kill_risk: If label-efficiency curves coincide, physical cues add nothing beyond existing pretraining, and the premise fails.
community_default_belief: Large-scale image-level pretraining plus full box supervision is the practical route to detection, with motion cues a historical curiosity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Image-level pretraining optimizes semantic invariance rather than instance delineation, leaving a localization-specific signal that only spatial physical cues supply cheaply.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Probe how well motion-derived masks align with ground-truth boxes on a video dataset; high alignment establishes the signal's ceiling before any pretraining investment.

title: Per-class oscillation diagnosis and selective weight averaging in long detection schedules
one_line_idea: Diagnose late-training per-class performance oscillation in detection fine-tuning and exploit it with class-aware checkpoint averaging instead of taking the final checkpoint.
problem: Long detection schedules show per-class metrics oscillating out of phase late in training, so any single checkpoint is suboptimal for many classes at once, and standard uniform weight averaging ignores this structure.
core_hypothesis: Late-phase per-class oscillations are real, systematic, and partially anti-correlated between class groups, enabling selective or weighted checkpoint combination that beats both the last checkpoint and uniform averaging.
core_claim: An oscillation-aware combination of late checkpoints yields consistent metric gains over standard checkpoint selection at zero training-cost increase.
method_sketch: Log per-class validation metrics across late checkpoints to characterize oscillation structure, then construct weighted averages or per-head stitching informed by the oscillation phases, validating on held-out data against last-checkpoint and uniform-average baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class late-phase oscillation amplitude will exceed seed-level noise for a substantial class fraction, and oscillation-aware combination will beat uniform averaging by a small but consistent margin across datasets.
why_important: It is a free-lunch improvement extractable from training runs everyone already performs, and it exposes an unexplained optimization phenomenon worth understanding.
why_possibly_novel: Weight averaging is standard, but per-class oscillation diagnosis driving structured combination in detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The checkpoints disagree class by class; harvest the disagreement.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log per-class metrics over the last quarter of one training run, quantify oscillation versus noise, and test simple oscillation-aware averaging against baselines.
main_risk: Oscillations may be mostly validation-set measurement noise rather than genuine parameter-space cycling.
kill_risk: If per-class trajectories are noise-dominated, there is no structure to exploit and the method reduces to uniform averaging.
community_default_belief: Late training is a smooth convergence, and uniform checkpoint averaging captures whatever variation remains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class gradients compete for shared capacity, and competition under a decaying learning rate plausibly produces structured cycling rather than smooth settling.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Plot per-class validation curves for the final epochs of any existing long run; visible anti-correlated swings across classes confirm the phenomenon from logs alone.

title: Reliability-weighted loss unifying label-noise estimates with example weighting
one_line_idea: Weight each annotation's loss contribution by an estimated reliability combining source, class, size, and agreement covariates, replacing uniform trust in every label.
problem: Training treats a box from a careless source, a tiny ambiguous object, and a triple-verified clean instance as equally authoritative targets, though their label reliabilities differ by large factors.
core_hypothesis: Per-annotation reliability is predictable from observable covariates, and reliability-weighted losses improve final performance over uniform weighting and over generic robust-loss functions that ignore covariates.
core_claim: A reliability model fitted on a verified subset and applied as loss weighting yields metric gains on clean evaluation, with the largest gains on datasets with heterogeneous annotation provenance.
method_sketch: Fit a reliability predictor from covariates using a human-verified calibration subset, weight classification and regression losses by predicted reliability with a floor to avoid discarding hard classes, and compare against uniform and robust-loss baselines on verification-cleaned evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Reliability weighting will outperform uniform weighting on heterogeneous-provenance data and remain neutral on uniformly clean data, isolating the mechanism to noise heterogeneity.
why_important: Production datasets are provenance mosaics, and a principled trust model converts known quality metadata into free performance.
why_possibly_novel: Robust losses and noise modeling exist separately, but covariate-driven per-annotation reliability weighting validated on cleaned detection evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Stop treating all labels as equally true; the metadata already says otherwise.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a merged multi-source dataset, fit the reliability model on a small verified sample, train weighted versus uniform twins, and evaluate on the cleaned subset.
main_risk: Reliability weighting may correlate with class and size, inadvertently down-weighting hard strata and recreating a long-tail problem.
kill_risk: If predicted reliability shows no relationship to verified label correctness, the covariates carry no trust signal and the scheme collapses.
community_default_belief: Robust loss functions and data scale adequately absorb annotation quality variation without explicit reliability modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generic robustness handles symmetric noise, but provenance-driven noise is structured and predictable, which uniform robustness cannot exploit.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On a verified sample, test whether source and size covariates predict label error with a simple classifier; predictive power justifies the full pipeline.

title: Oracle-matching experiment to isolate the true bottleneck of one-to-one assignment training
one_line_idea: Feed set-prediction detectors an oracle-stabilized matching during training to cleanly separate matching-instability harm from gradient-sparsity harm, resolving why auxiliary one-to-many tricks work.
problem: Auxiliary one-to-many supervision empirically accelerates set-prediction detector training, but the field cannot say whether the benefit comes from denser gradients or from stabilizing the assignment, so remedy design is guesswork.
core_hypothesis: Matching instability, not gradient sparsity, is the dominant cost of one-to-one training, which an oracle experiment fixing assignments across iterations can demonstrate by recovering most of the auxiliary-supervision benefit without any extra gradient density.
core_claim: A controlled study with frozen or smoothed matchings will attribute the convergence gap between one-to-one and one-to-many training to its actual cause, yielding a principled lightweight stabilizer as a byproduct.
method_sketch: Train variants with standard matching, temporally smoothed matching, periodically frozen matching, and one-to-many auxiliaries at equal compute, measure convergence speed and final metrics, and attribute effects via this factorial design.
falsifiable_prediction: Matching stabilization alone will recover the majority of the auxiliary-supervision convergence benefit, while added gradient density with unstable matching will recover a minority.
why_important: The result redirects architecture effort for the dominant detector family from supervision densification toward assignment stabilization, or vice versa, with evidence instead of fashion.
why_possibly_novel: Both phenomena are discussed, but a factorial oracle-style attribution experiment appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Run the control experiment the auxiliary-loss literature skipped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement smoothed and frozen matching variants on one set-prediction detector and compare convergence against standard and auxiliary-supervised baselines at matched compute.
main_risk: Frozen matchings may introduce their own pathology, confounding the attribution the experiment is meant to clean up.
kill_risk: If neither stabilization nor densification alone recovers the benefit, the two-factor framing is wrong and the interaction matters, complicating the story.
community_default_belief: Auxiliary one-to-many supervision works because sparse one-to-one gradients starve the model of training signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The sparse-gradient story ignores that assignments also flip-flop across iterations, injecting target noise that alone could explain slow convergence.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure assignment flip rates across consecutive iterations in a standard run; near-zero flip rates would immediately refute the instability account.

title: Instance discriminability versus spatial equivariance tradeoff in pretraining for detection
one_line_idea: Define and measure a two-axis diagnostic, instance discriminability and spatial equivariance, on pretrained backbones, and show it predicts detection transfer better than classification accuracy.
problem: Backbones are selected for detection by upstream classification accuracy, which measures invariance, while detection needs precisely the spatial equivariance that invariance-oriented pretraining destroys.
core_hypothesis: Detection fine-tuning performance is governed by a balance of two measurable feature properties, and pretraining objectives sit at different points on this tradeoff, explaining known anomalies where worse classifiers make better detection backbones.
core_claim: A cheap probe suite measuring both axes on frozen features will predict downstream detection quality across diverse pretraining recipes better than upstream accuracy, enabling probe-guided pretraining selection without fine-tuning sweeps.
method_sketch: Design probes for localization equivariance and instance separation on frozen features, evaluate across many public pretrained backbones, fine-tune all on standard detection, and compare predictive power of the probes against upstream accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Probe-based prediction will rank backbones for detection transfer with substantially higher correlation than upstream classification accuracy does across pretraining families.
why_important: Backbone selection and pretraining design currently optimize a misaligned proxy, and a correct cheap predictor changes both research and practice.
why_possibly_novel: Individual probing studies exist, but a validated two-axis predictor spanning pretraining families for detection transfer appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Score pretraining by what detection needs, not by classification accuracy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe a dozen public backbones, fine-tune each on one detection benchmark under one recipe, and compare rank correlations of the two predictors.
main_risk: Fine-tuning may partially repair feature deficiencies, weakening the frozen-probe signal's predictive value.
kill_risk: If upstream accuracy predicts transfer as well as the probes, the diagnostic adds no information and the misalignment story is overblown.
community_default_belief: Better classification pretraining means a better detection backbone, up to modest architecture caveats.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Invariance training explicitly discards spatial information that detection must reconstruct, a structural conflict classification accuracy cannot reflect.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare two backbones with similar accuracy but different objectives on the probes and one quick detection fine-tune; divergence between probe and accuracy predictions shows immediately.

title: Scaling-law decomposition for detection pretraining data value
one_line_idea: Fit detection-transfer scaling curves separately for pretraining data quantity, domain proximity, and supervision type, testing whether box-supervised pretraining saturates far earlier than the field's data appetite assumes.
problem: Detection data budgets are allocated by classification-era intuitions, without measured scaling curves that decompose the marginal value of more pretraining data by supervision type and domain match to the target task.
core_hypothesis: Detection fine-tune performance follows measurable saturating curves in pretraining scale, with saturation arriving earlier for box-supervised pretraining than image-level pretraining, and domain proximity shifting curves more than raw quantity beyond moderate scale.
core_claim: A controlled scaling study across pretraining sizes, supervision types, and domain mixes will yield transferable allocation rules that beat quantity-maximizing defaults at fixed budget.
method_sketch: Pretrain matched backbones across a grid of data scales, supervision types, and domain mixes within accessible compute, fine-tune on several detection targets, fit parametric scaling curves, and validate allocation predictions on a held-out budget scenario.
falsifiable_prediction: Marginal gains from box-supervised pretraining scale will fall below domain-proximity gains beyond a moderate scale threshold, and curve-based allocation will outperform naive maximum-data allocation at equal cost.
why_important: Data acquisition is the dominant cost lever in detection, and unmeasured scaling assumptions currently steer very large investments.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling laws are established for language and image classification, but a decomposition targeted at detection transfer with allocation validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Measure the exchange rates among quantity, domain, and supervision for detection instead of assuming them.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a reduced grid, three scales, two supervision types, two domain mixes, on one target benchmark and check whether fitted curves are stable and predictive on one held-out configuration.
main_risk: Findings at accessible compute may extrapolate poorly to industrial scale, limiting authority of the allocation rules.
kill_risk: If curves fail to fit or predictions miss the held-out configuration, the parametric framework is inadequate and conclusions are unsafe.
community_default_belief: More pretraining data reliably helps detection, and bigger is the safe default for data budgets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transfer value saturates in supervision-specific ways, and past the knee the same budget spent on domain-matched or better-quality data plausibly dominates.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fine-tune from checkpoints pretrained at two very different scales of the same corpus onto one target; a negligible gap at the target immediately evidences saturation.

title: Layer-wise probing to place minimal detection adapters on frozen foundation backbones
one_line_idea: Use layer-wise probes to find where detection-relevant information already exists in frozen foundation backbones, then place minimal adapters exactly there instead of fine-tuning everything.
problem: Detection fine-tuning updates entire backbones by default, but if most detection-relevant information is already linearly accessible at specific layers, full fine-tuning wastes compute and destroys general features for marginal gain.
core_hypothesis: Detection-relevant signals concentrate at identifiable layers of foundation backbones, and probe-guided adapter placement recovers nearly full fine-tuning performance at a small fraction of trainable parameters, beating uniform adapter placement.
core_claim: A probing-then-placement policy produces adapter configurations that dominate uniform and heuristic placements on the accuracy-per-trainable-parameter frontier for detection transfer.
method_sketch: Probe frozen layers for localization and instance-classification signals, rank layers by probe headroom, place capacity-matched adapters according to the ranking, and compare against uniform placement and full fine-tuning across parameter budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Probe-guided placement will reach a target fraction of full fine-tuning performance with clearly fewer trainable parameters than uniform placement across backbones.
why_important: Foundation-backbone reuse is the dominant paradigm, and principled adapter placement converts probing insight directly into compute savings for every downstream detection user.
why_possibly_novel: Adapters and probing both exist; a validated probe-to-placement policy for detection transfer appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let measurements, not habit, decide where the trainable parameters go.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one frozen backbone and one benchmark, compare probe-guided versus uniform adapter placement at two parameter budgets.
main_risk: Probe accuracy on frozen features may mispredict where adapters help once layers interact under training.
kill_risk: If placement makes no difference at matched budgets, adapter position is a free variable and the probing step is wasted effort.
community_default_belief: Where adapters go matters less than how many parameters they add, and full fine-tuning remains the safe maximum-performance choice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Information relevant to detection is unevenly distributed across depth, so position determines whether added capacity edits the right computations.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare detection heads trained on features from two different frozen layers of one backbone; large performance differences establish position sensitivity in a day.

title: Procedural shape-and-layout pretraining for detection priors
one_line_idea: Pretrain detectors on procedurally generated abstract scenes of shapes with controlled occlusion, crowding, and scale statistics, testing whether detection-specific priors transfer to real data without any real images.
problem: Detection pretraining conflates learning natural image statistics with learning detection-structural skills like occlusion handling and instance separation, so nobody knows how much of pretraining value is the latter, cheaply synthesizable part.
core_hypothesis: A measurable share of detection pretraining benefit comes from structural skills learnable from abstract procedural scenes, and such pretraining provides real transfer gains, especially in low-label regimes, at essentially zero data cost.
core_claim: Procedural-scene pretraining will beat random initialization by a clear margin on real detection fine-tuning, and combining it with image-level pretraining will beat image-level pretraining alone, isolating a structural-skill component.
method_sketch: Generate abstract multi-object scenes with parameterized crowding, occlusion, and scale distributions, pretrain standard detectors on them, fine-tune on real benchmarks at multiple label budgets, and ablate which procedural statistics drive transfer.
falsifiable_prediction: Procedural pretraining will improve low-label fine-tuning markedly, with gains sensitive to matching procedural crowding and scale statistics to the target domain.
why_important: It would isolate what part of detection competence is data-free and open a controllable, bias-free pretraining channel every lab can afford.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic pretraining with abstract patterns exists for classification; a detection-structural version with statistic-matching ablations appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Teach occlusion and instance separation with geometry alone, before showing the model a single photograph.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain one detector on procedural scenes, fine-tune on one benchmark at a low label budget, and compare against random-init and image-pretrained controls.
main_risk: The domain gap from abstract shapes may be too large for modern backbones to retain anything useful through fine-tuning.
kill_risk: If procedural pretraining matches random initialization after fine-tuning, no structural skill survives transfer and the hypothesis is dead.
community_default_belief: Pretraining value comes from natural image statistics at scale; abstract synthetic data cannot substitute for real-world visual experience.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection has task-structural components, occlusion logic, crowd separation, scale handling, that are domain-independent and thus learnable from any data exhibiting the structure.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Short pretraining on procedural scenes followed by a quick low-label fine-tune against random init; the gap appears within a few GPU-days.

title: Quality-quantity exchange rates for tracking-derived pseudo-box pretraining
one_line_idea: Quantify how many motion-and-tracking-derived pseudo-boxes from unlabeled video equal one human-annotated box for detection pretraining value, establishing exchange rates that make data planning quantitative.
problem: Unlabeled video can yield unlimited noisy pseudo-boxes via motion segmentation and tracking, but without a measured quality-quantity exchange rate against human boxes, teams cannot rationally allocate between annotation budgets and video mining.
core_hypothesis: Pretraining value follows a predictable curve in pseudo-box noise level and volume, yielding stable exchange rates, and mined video boxes at realistic noise levels are worth a meaningful fraction of human boxes for downstream transfer.
core_claim: A controlled study varying pseudo-box volume and verified noise level against human-box controls will produce exchange-rate curves that hold across at least two target benchmarks.
method_sketch: Mine pseudo-boxes from unlabeled video at scale, characterize their noise against a verified sample, pretrain detectors on grids of volume and noise, fine-tune on target benchmarks, and fit value curves relative to human-box pretraining controls.
falsifiable_prediction: The fitted exchange rate will be stable across benchmarks within a factor and will show mined boxes retaining substantial value up to surprisingly high noise levels before value collapses.
why_important: It converts the perennial cheap-data-versus-clean-data debate for detection into a measured planning tool with direct budget consequences.
why_possibly_novel: Pseudo-label pretraining is common, but measured exchange-rate curves against human annotation for detection appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Put a price tag on noisy free data, in units of human boxes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain at three pseudo-box volumes and two noise levels, fine-tune on one benchmark, and check whether a consistent exchange rate fits the results.
main_risk: Exchange rates may vary strongly with target-domain similarity to the mined video, complicating a single-number summary.
kill_risk: If value curves are erratic and no stable exchange rate exists, the planning-tool framing fails even if pseudo-boxes help on average.
community_default_belief: Noisy pseudo-labels are a poor substitute for human annotation and mainly useful as a marginal supplement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pretraining is noise-tolerant in ways fine-tuning is not, so the substitution rate may be far more favorable than annotation-era intuitions suggest.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare fine-tune transfer from equal-compute pretraining on mined boxes versus a fraction-sized human-box corpus; the first exchange-rate point falls out of one comparison.

title: Multi-resolution pretraining to close the resolution mismatch with detection fine-tuning
one_line_idea: Pretrain backbones with explicit multi-resolution schedules so detection fine-tuning at high resolution stops paying an adaptation tax that positional-embedding interpolation does not cover.
problem: Backbones are pretrained at low resolution and detection fine-tunes at much higher resolution, with the mismatch papered over by positional-embedding interpolation whose adequacy for spatial tasks is assumed, not measured.
core_hypothesis: Resolution mismatch causes a persistent, small-object-concentrated transfer penalty that interpolation does not repair, and mixing resolutions during pretraining removes the penalty at modest pretraining cost.
core_claim: Multi-resolution pretraining will improve detection transfer, with gains concentrated in small-object strata and growing with the pretrain-finetune resolution gap, while matched-compute single-resolution pretraining will not.
method_sketch: Pretrain twins with single- and mixed-resolution schedules at matched compute, fine-tune on detection at several resolutions, and decompose transfer gaps by object size and by attention-pattern drift between resolutions.
falsifiable_prediction: The mixed-resolution backbone will show smaller performance drops as fine-tuning resolution deviates from pretraining resolution, and the advantage will localize in small-object metrics.
why_important: Every detection pipeline built on pretrained backbones inherits this mismatch, so a validated fix has near-universal applicability.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution adaptation tricks exist, but a controlled study establishing the mismatch cost and its removal via pretraining schedule for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Make resolution a pretraining distribution, not a fixed constant to be interpolated later.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain small twins under the two schedules, fine-tune on one benchmark at two resolutions, and compare size-stratified transfer.
main_risk: At matched compute, mixed-resolution pretraining sees fewer high-resolution tokens overall, potentially trading one deficiency for another.
kill_risk: If single-resolution pretraining plus interpolation shows no measurable small-object penalty, the mismatch tax does not exist and the fix is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Positional-embedding interpolation adequately handles pretrain-to-finetune resolution changes for downstream spatial tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interpolation adjusts embeddings but not the resolution-conditioned statistics of learned attention and features, which spatial tasks are sensitive to.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate a frozen pretrained backbone's detection-probe quality at multiple input resolutions; a sharp degradation away from the pretraining resolution demonstrates the unrepaired mismatch.

title: Decomposing whether text supervision improves locating or only naming
one_line_idea: Design controlled comparisons that separate localization improvement from naming improvement when adding region-text supervision, testing the suspicion that text teaches names but contributes little to spatial ability.
problem: Region-text pretraining is credited with broad detection improvements, but its gains conflate two mechanisms, better spatial localization and better semantic naming, and the field has not measured their separate contributions.
core_hypothesis: Text supervision predominantly improves naming, with class-agnostic localization quality driven almost entirely by the visual and box supervision, implying cheaper visual-only data can replace text data for the localization half.
core_claim: A factorial study crossing localization supervision with naming supervision will show near-zero interaction on class-agnostic localization metrics and strong text effects only on naming metrics.
method_sketch: Train matched models with and without text supervision while holding box supervision constant, evaluate class-agnostic proposal quality and naming accuracy separately, and test transfer of each component to new domains.
falsifiable_prediction: Class-agnostic localization metrics will be statistically indistinguishable with and without text supervision at matched visual data, while naming metrics will differ strongly.
why_important: If localization needs no text, data strategies for the expensive text-paired collection can be refocused on naming coverage alone, changing acquisition economics.
why_possibly_novel: Ablations exist within individual systems, but a clean factorial decomposition of text supervision's mechanism for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ask what the words actually teach the boxes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train two matched models differing only in text supervision on moderate-scale data and compare class-agnostic proposal recall and naming accuracy.
main_risk: Text data may bring extra image diversity as a hidden confound unless corpora are carefully matched.
kill_risk: If text supervision clearly improves class-agnostic localization, the naming-only hypothesis is dead and text data is validated as spatially useful.
community_default_belief: Web-scale text supervision improves detection holistically, including where objects are found, not just what they are called.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Captions rarely encode precise spatial extents, so the gradient signal they provide about localization is indirect at best and plausibly negligible.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare proposal-stage recall of public detector pairs that differ mainly in text-supervision scale; a persistent recall gap would immediately challenge the naming-only view.

title: Mask-free calibration phase for masked-image-modeling backbones in detection
one_line_idea: Insert a brief mask-free feature-calibration phase between masked-image pretraining and detection fine-tuning, correcting the train-inference mismatch of features shaped by mask tokens.
problem: Masked-image-modeling backbones learn feature statistics in the presence of mask tokens, but detection fine-tuning and inference never mask, and the resulting distributional mismatch is absorbed blindly by fine-tuning rather than corrected deliberately.
core_hypothesis: The mask-conditioned feature mismatch measurably distorts early fine-tuning and a short self-supervised mask-free calibration phase, aligning feature statistics without labels, improves final detection transfer and stability.
core_claim: Calibration-then-finetune will beat direct fine-tuning at matched total compute, with the largest gains at short fine-tuning budgets and for localization-sensitive metrics.
method_sketch: Measure feature-statistic differences between masked and unmasked forward passes of pretrained backbones, run a brief mask-free objective such as feature self-distillation, then fine-tune on detection and compare against direct fine-tuning at equal compute.
falsifiable_prediction: Masked-versus-unmasked feature statistics will differ measurably, and the calibration phase will improve detection metrics under short fine-tuning schedules while converging to parity at very long schedules.
why_important: Masked pretraining is a dominant recipe and detection its major consumer, so even small systematic transfer losses from the mismatch are widely multiplied.
why_possibly_novel: The masked-pretraining mismatch is occasionally noted, but a deliberate calibration phase evaluated for detection transfer appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: De-mask the features before asking them to localize.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantify the masked-unmasked feature gap on one pretrained backbone, run a short calibration, and compare short-schedule detection fine-tunes with and without it.
main_risk: Long fine-tuning may fully absorb the mismatch anyway, confining benefits to budget-constrained settings.
kill_risk: If masked and unmasked feature statistics are already nearly identical, there is no mismatch to calibrate and the premise is void.
community_default_belief: Fine-tuning transparently handles any pretraining artifacts, making explicit calibration phases unnecessary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning spends its early updates undoing the mismatch with labeled data, an expensive correction that unlabeled calibration could do for free.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare channel statistics of a pretrained backbone under masked versus unmasked inputs; the gap size, computable in hours, determines whether calibration has a target.

title: Localization-uncertainty gating as the primary deployment filter
one_line_idea: Gate deployed detections on heteroscedastic localization uncertainty rather than class confidence, testing which uncertainty better triages errors for downstream consumers.
problem: Deployments filter detections by class score alone, though localization errors, wrong extents and drifted boxes, are often the operationally damaging ones and are invisible to classification confidence.
core_hypothesis: Predicted per-coordinate localization variance carries error-triage information complementary to class score, and gating on a combined signal dominates class-score gating on deployment-relevant error metrics.
core_claim: A detector with a calibrated heteroscedastic box head enables filtering rules that reduce high-cost localization failures at fixed detection yield compared with class-score-only filtering.
method_sketch: Train standard detectors with variance-predicting box heads, calibrate the variances post hoc, define combined gating rules, and evaluate triage quality via risk-coverage curves for localization-critical error definitions on multiple benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Risk-coverage curves for combined gating will dominate class-score gating whenever the error definition includes localization quality, with the largest margins on small and occluded objects.
why_important: Downstream consumers like trackers and planners fail on bad boxes, not just on wrong classes, and current filtering is blind to exactly that failure channel.
why_possibly_novel: Uncertainty box heads exist, but their use as primary deployment gates with risk-coverage validation against score gating appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Filter on how sure the box is, not just how sure the name is.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Add a variance head to one detector, calibrate on validation data, and compare risk-coverage curves of the two gating rules for a localization-weighted error definition.
main_risk: Predicted variances may be poorly calibrated out of distribution, exactly where gating matters most.
kill_risk: If localization variance is essentially redundant with class score for triage, combined gating adds nothing.
community_default_belief: Class confidence is the operative reliability signal for detections, and box uncertainty is a research nicety.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Classification and localization error channels are weakly coupled, so a one-channel gate must miss much of the second channel's risk.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate class score with actual localization error on any benchmark's cached detections; a weak correlation immediately shows headroom for a second gating signal.

title: Training an explicit none-of-the-above head from annotation ignore regions
one_line_idea: Use the ignore regions and skipped ambiguous zones that already exist in detection datasets as free supervision for an explicit unknown-object head, gaining open-world recall without new labels.
problem: Detectors either suppress unknown objects as background or hallucinate known classes onto them, and open-world methods typically require new annotation efforts while datasets already contain ignore regions marking exactly the ambiguous stuff.
core_hypothesis: Ignore regions are a usable, cost-free training distribution for unknown objectness, and a head trained to fire on them generalizes to genuinely novel objects at test time without harming known-class precision.
core_claim: An unknown head supervised on existing ignore annotations improves unknown-object recall on open-world evaluations while leaving known-class metrics within noise of the baseline.
method_sketch: Extract ignore and crowd regions from standard datasets, train an auxiliary objectness-without-class head on them alongside normal detection, evaluate on open-world protocols with held-out classes as unknowns, and ablate against energy-based unknown scoring.
falsifiable_prediction: The ignore-trained head will recall a substantially higher fraction of held-out-class objects than background-suppression baselines and energy-score baselines at matched false-positive budgets.
why_important: It converts a universally present annotation byproduct into open-world capability, lowering the entry cost of unknown-aware detection to zero new labels.
why_possibly_novel: Ignore regions are treated as loss masks; as positive supervision for an unknown class they appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The dataset already annotates the unknown; it just calls it ignore.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the auxiliary head on one dataset's ignore regions and evaluate held-out-class recall against baselines under a standard open-world protocol.
main_risk: Ignore regions conflate crowds of known classes with true ambiguity, potentially teaching the head to fire on crowded known objects.
kill_risk: If the head's unknown recall matches energy-score baselines without exceeding them, the free supervision carries no additional signal.
community_default_belief: Open-world detection requires dedicated unknown annotation or sophisticated post-hoc scoring; standard datasets contain no unknown supervision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ignore annotations are precisely human judgments of not-confidently-any-class, which is operationally the definition of the unknown supervision the field says it lacks.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure how often held-out-class objects fall inside ignore-like feature regions of a trained baseline by probing; quick evidence for whether the distributions align.

title: Predicting per-class shift fragility from feature-space compactness
one_line_idea: Predict which classes will degrade most under distribution shift from their training-time feature-space geometry, enabling monitoring budgets to be allocated before any shifted data exists.
problem: Detector degradation under shift is strongly class-dependent, but deployments discover which classes break only after failures occur, lacking any a priori fragility estimate.
core_hypothesis: Classes with less compact, lower-margin feature distributions at training time degrade disproportionately under distribution shift, making per-class fragility predictable from training data alone.
core_claim: A fragility score computed from per-class feature compactness and boundary margin will rank-correlate strongly with per-class performance drops across multiple real and synthetic shifts.
method_sketch: Compute per-class feature statistics from a trained detector on clean data, define candidate fragility scores, evaluate the same detector across corruption and natural-shift suites, and test rank correlation between predicted and observed per-class drops.
falsifiable_prediction: Fragility rankings will achieve strong positive rank correlation with observed per-class degradation across at least two independent shift types, far above frequency-based or accuracy-based baselines.
why_important: It enables preemptive monitoring and targeted data collection for exactly the classes that will fail, before deployment sees a single shifted example.
why_possibly_novel: Shift robustness prediction exists at the dataset level, but per-class fragility forecasting from feature geometry for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Forecast the per-class failure profile of a shift you have never seen.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one detector, compute fragility scores and evaluate per-class drops on one corruption suite and one natural-shift dataset, reporting rank correlations against baselines.
main_risk: Different shift types may break different classes, making a single geometry-based score insufficient across shift families.
kill_risk: If correlations are near zero or unstable across shifts, feature geometry does not encode fragility and the forecasting premise dies.
community_default_belief: Robustness is a global model property, and per-class shift behavior is unpredictable without shifted validation data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Degradation mechanics plausibly run through decision-boundary geometry, which is fully observable at training time and class-resolved.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate per-class clean-feature compactness with per-class corruption drops for one public detector; cached features and standard suites answer it in a day.

title: Conformal detection sets with box-level nonconformity and coverage guarantees
one_line_idea: Define box-level nonconformity scores that make conformal prediction work for detection, producing per-image detection sets with distribution-free miss-rate guarantees.
problem: Safety-critical consumers need guarantees like at most a specified fraction of true objects missed, but detection outputs carry no statistical guarantees and conformal methods lack a canonical extension to variable-size, structured detection outputs.
core_hypothesis: A nonconformity design combining score thresholds with localization tolerance bands admits valid conformal calibration for detection, yielding guaranteed recall sets whose size remains practically useful.
core_claim: The proposed conformal wrapper achieves target object-level coverage empirically on exchangeable splits while inflating detection-set size manageably, and degrades gracefully under mild shift with reweighting.
method_sketch: Define object-level nonconformity via the minimal score threshold that still captures each ground truth within a localization tolerance, calibrate quantiles on held-out data, emit augmented detection sets at deployment, and study set-size versus coverage tradeoffs.
falsifiable_prediction: Empirical coverage will match nominal targets within statistical tolerance on exchangeable data, and set sizes will remain within a small multiple of standard output sizes at practical coverage levels.
why_important: Guaranteed-recall detection is a prerequisite for certification arguments in medical and autonomous domains, and currently nothing offers it.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal object detection has early explorations, but a tolerance-banded object-level nonconformity with practical set-size analysis appears underdeveloped (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Distribution-free recall guarantees as a wrapper around any detector.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the wrapper on one detector and benchmark, verify coverage on repeated calibration-test splits, and report set-size distributions.
main_risk: Guarantees hold under exchangeability, which deployment shift violates, requiring honest scoping of claims.
kill_risk: If achieving useful coverage requires absurdly large detection sets, the guarantee is vacuous in practice.
community_default_belief: Detection uncertainty is handled with heuristic score thresholds, and formal guarantees are unattainable for structured outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conformal machinery requires only a scalar nonconformity per object, which detection can define, making the unattainability assumption a failure of formulation rather than of possibility.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Calibrate the simplest score-threshold nonconformity on one dataset split and check empirical coverage; validity or violation appears within a day.

title: Propagating suppression ambiguity into final detection confidences
one_line_idea: Make the suppression stage output uncertainty about its own keep-or-merge decisions, flagging duplicate-versus-distinct ambiguity that downstream consumers currently never see.
problem: Suppression silently commits to whether overlapping candidates are one object or two, and its mistakes, merged neighbors or duplicated singletons, reach consumers with full confidence and no trace of the ambiguity.
core_hypothesis: Keep-or-merge ambiguity is quantifiable from the local candidate configuration, and exposing it as a per-detection annotation improves downstream decisions like tracking association and human review routing.
core_claim: An ambiguity-annotated suppression stage identifies the majority of merge and duplication errors at low flag rates, and a tracker consuming the flags reduces identity errors in crowded scenes.
method_sketch: Model suppression decisions probabilistically from candidate score-overlap configurations, calibrate ambiguity against ground-truth merge and duplicate errors, expose flags in the output format, and integrate with a standard tracker for downstream validation.
falsifiable_prediction: Flagged detections will contain most suppression-caused errors at a flag rate below a practical review budget, and flag-aware tracking will measurably cut identity switches in dense sequences.
why_important: Suppression errors are a known silent failure channel in crowds, and surfacing them converts unrecoverable mistakes into reviewable or recoverable ones.
why_possibly_novel: Soft suppression variants exist for accuracy, but exporting calibrated suppression ambiguity as a consumer-facing signal appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let the pipeline confess where it guessed one-versus-two.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate an ambiguity score on one crowded dataset, measure error capture versus flag rate, and run one tracker with and without flags.
main_risk: Downstream systems may lack mechanisms to exploit flags, limiting demonstrable end-to-end value.
kill_risk: If suppression errors are spread uniformly over unflaggable configurations, ambiguity is not locally quantifiable and the signal fails.
community_default_belief: Suppression is a deterministic cleanup step whose internal decisions need no uncertainty treatment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In crowded configurations the one-versus-two question is genuinely underdetermined by the candidate set, which is the textbook case for exposing rather than hiding uncertainty.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On a crowded validation set, check whether merge and duplicate errors concentrate in identifiable score-overlap configurations; a quick clustering of error contexts answers it.

title: Position-prior debiasing for spatially out-of-distribution objects
one_line_idea: Measure how much detectors depend on where classes usually appear in the frame and debias training so known classes in unusual positions and sizes stop being missed.
problem: Detectors absorb dataset-specific position and size priors, so a perfectly visible object in an unusual location, a pedestrian on a highway gantry, a car on a rooftop, gets missed for reasons invisible to standard evaluation.
core_hypothesis: Spatial priors contribute a measurable share of detection decisions, and prior-randomizing augmentation or explicit prior-factorized scoring removes the dependence at minor cost on prior-consistent data.
core_claim: A spatial-out-of-distribution test suite will document large recall drops for prior-violating placements, and debiased training will cut those drops by a large fraction while losing little on standard benchmarks.
method_sketch: Quantify per-class position-size priors from training data, build an evaluation suite of real and composited prior-violating instances, train with placement-randomized augmentation and a factorized score that separates appearance evidence from spatial prior, and compare recall on the suite.
falsifiable_prediction: Baseline recall on prior-violating placements will be dramatically below matched prior-consistent recall, and debiased models will close most of the gap with under a point of aggregate benchmark cost.
why_important: Prior-violating placements are precisely the anomalous scenarios where safety systems must not fail, and current training makes failure there systematic.
why_possibly_novel: Context bias is studied broadly, but a position-size prior audit with factorized-score debiasing for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Detectors have a where-things-belong prejudice; measure it and train it out.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite a few hundred prior-violating instances for three classes, measure baseline recall gaps, and retrain with placement randomization to re-measure.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts may exaggerate baseline failures, requiring some real prior-violating imagery for validation.
kill_risk: If baseline recall on prior-violating placements is already near normal, spatial priors are weak and the debiasing solves a non-problem.
community_default_belief: Detectors detect objects wherever they appear, with spatial context a mild secondary influence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training distributions have strong position regularities, and nothing in the objective discourages exploiting them as decision evidence.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Paste normal-scale instances of one class into unusual frame positions and measure recall change with a frozen detector; the gap quantifies prior dependence in hours.
