title: Budgeted-abstention evaluation for human-AI detection teams
one_line_idea: Evaluate detectors by team performance when they may flag a budgeted fraction of uncertain detections for human resolution, measuring the flag-quality skill that solo metrics ignore.
problem: Deployed detection is usually human-in-the-loop, yet benchmarks score models solo, so a model that knows what to escalate is indistinguishable from one that is confidently wrong on the same items.
core_hypothesis: Models differ substantially in escalation quality at matched solo accuracy, and a budgeted-abstention protocol reveals this difference and predicts real human-AI team outcomes.
core_claim: A standardized protocol scoring team accuracy versus escalation budget will reorder models relative to solo metrics and correlate with measured human-team performance in a user study.
method_sketch: Define escalation as sending flagged detections and regions to an oracle or human, sweep budgets, compute team-accuracy curves for public models with various uncertainty signals, and validate against a small real-user study.
falsifiable_prediction: Team-accuracy curves will cross solo-metric rankings for some model pairs, and curve ordering will match the user-study ordering better than solo metrics do.
why_important: Escalation quality is the property that determines real operational value in monitored deployments, and it is currently unmeasured and thus unoptimized.
why_possibly_novel: Selective prediction is studied in classification, but a budgeted team-evaluation protocol with human validation for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Benchmark the model as a teammate, not a soloist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute team-accuracy curves under oracle resolution for three public detectors with different uncertainty signals on one benchmark and test for ranking changes.
main_risk: Oracle-resolution results may overstate achievable human performance, requiring the user study to anchor realism.
kill_risk: If team curves are fully determined by solo accuracy across models, escalation skill does not vary and the protocol measures nothing new.
community_default_belief: Improving solo accuracy is the path to deployment value, and abstention mechanisms are peripheral conveniences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At matched accuracy, knowing-when-wrong varies widely, and in monitored pipelines that variation converts directly into team output quality.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For two detectors with similar benchmark scores, compare error concentration in their lowest-confidence decile; different concentrations prove differing escalation potential immediately.

title: Region-level active learning to replace image-level selection in detection annotation
one_line_idea: Select and annotate informative regions rather than whole images in detection active learning, since most pixels of a selected image carry no information worth its annotation cost.
problem: Detection active learning selects whole images, but informativeness is spatially concentrated, so budgets are spent annotating easy or empty regions bundled with the informative ones.
core_hypothesis: Region-granular selection with partial-image annotation and missing-label-aware training achieves target performance at a substantially lower annotation cost than image-level selection under identical uncertainty signals.
core_claim: At matched measured annotation cost in human time, region-level active learning reaches performance milestones faster than image-level selection across multiple rounds and datasets.
method_sketch: Score spatial uncertainty maps, select region proposals under a cost model calibrated in annotator seconds, annotate only selected regions, train with masking for unannotated areas, and run multi-round comparisons against image-level baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Region selection will show a clear annotation-cost advantage to fixed milestones, with the advantage growing on datasets with spatially sparse difficulty.
why_important: Annotation budget is the binding constraint of applied detection, and granularity of selection is a large, mostly unclaimed efficiency lever.
why_possibly_novel: Region-level ideas appear in fragments, but cost-calibrated multi-round comparisons with missing-label-aware training appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Stop buying whole images when you only need a corner.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two active-learning rounds on one dataset with simulated region annotation and a seconds-based cost model, comparing milestone costs against image-level selection.
main_risk: Partial annotation creates missing-label training hazards that could erase selection gains if handled naively.
kill_risk: If informative regions are so correlated within images that image selection captures them anyway, granularity buys nothing.
community_default_belief: Active learning for detection operates at image granularity because annotation workflows and training pipelines require complete images.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both the workflow and pipeline constraints are soft engineering conventions, while the informativeness concentration is a hard statistical fact favoring finer granularity.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure what fraction of an uncertainty map's total mass falls in the top decile of regions across a dataset; strong concentration validates the premise in hours.

title: Recall-safe objectness-gated token pruning for transformer detectors
one_line_idea: Prune background tokens early in transformer detectors using a cheap high-recall objectness gate with an explicit recall-safety constraint, rather than saliency heuristics with no miss guarantees.
problem: Most tokens in detection inputs are background, but existing token-pruning methods optimize aggregate accuracy and silently sacrifice small-object recall, making them unusable where misses are costly.
core_hypothesis: A gate trained explicitly for near-perfect object coverage at high pruning rates exists at trivial compute cost, enabling large end-to-end speedups with bounded, measurable recall loss concentrated nowhere in particular.
core_claim: Recall-constrained gating achieves a large token reduction with small-object recall preserved within a stated tolerance, dominating magnitude- and attention-based pruning at matched speedup.
method_sketch: Train a very small early-feature gate with a loss that heavily penalizes pruning any token overlapping annotated objects, calibrate a pruning threshold to a target coverage on validation data, and measure speedup and size-stratified recall against pruning baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched wall-clock speedups, the recall-safe gate will retain small-object recall within the calibrated tolerance while baseline pruning shows visibly larger small-object losses.
why_important: Token pruning is the main efficiency lever for transformer detectors, and its current recall-blindness blocks adoption in exactly the applications that need speed most.
why_possibly_novel: Token pruning is well studied for classification; recall-safety as an explicit calibrated constraint for detection pruning appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Prune with a coverage contract, not a saliency guess.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the gate on one benchmark, calibrate to a coverage target, and compare against attention-based pruning at equal speedup with size-stratified recall reporting.
main_risk: Coverage calibrated on one distribution may not transfer under domain shift, silently voiding the safety property.
kill_risk: If high-recall gating is impossible below moderate pruning rates, the speed-safety combination the idea promises cannot exist.
community_default_belief: Aggressive token pruning necessarily trades away hard-case accuracy, and aggregate-metric evaluation of pruning is adequate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregate evaluation hides that current losses concentrate on small objects, and nothing fundamental prevents a gate optimized for coverage rather than average saliency.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an existing pruning method with size-stratified recall on one benchmark; revealing concentrated small-object loss both motivates and baselines the work in hours.

title: Per-image resolution routing from a learned difficulty estimator
one_line_idea: Route each image to the cheapest input resolution predicted to preserve its detection quality, exploiting the fact that most images need far less resolution than the worst-case setting all images currently pay for.
problem: Deployments fix one input resolution sized for the hardest images, so the easy majority is processed at wasteful cost, yet no standard component predicts per-image resolution needs.
core_hypothesis: Per-image minimal sufficient resolution is predictable from cheap low-resolution features, and routing on this prediction preserves nearly all accuracy at a large average-compute reduction.
core_claim: A difficulty-estimator router will cut average inference cost substantially at negligible metric loss, outperforming random and heuristic routing at matched compute across benchmarks.
method_sketch: Label training images with their empirically minimal sufficient resolution by evaluating a detector across resolutions, train a lightweight estimator from thumbnail features to predict it, route at inference, and measure accuracy-compute frontiers against fixed-resolution baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: The routed system will retain the vast majority of full-resolution accuracy at a large fraction of compute saved, and routing errors will concentrate on a small, characterizable image subset.
why_important: Inference cost dominates detection deployment economics at scale, and per-input adaptivity is standard elsewhere but missing from mainstream detection serving.
why_possibly_novel: Dynamic-resolution ideas exist in efficient-vision literature, but sufficiency-labeled training of an explicit router with frontier evaluation for detection appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Spend resolution where the image, not the worst case, demands it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build sufficiency labels for one dataset, train the router, and compare routed frontiers against fixed resolutions on held-out data.
main_risk: Sufficiency labels depend on the specific detector, potentially requiring router retraining per model version.
kill_risk: If minimal sufficient resolution is unpredictable from cheap features, routing decisions are guesses and the frontier gains vanish.
community_default_belief: A single well-chosen input resolution is the practical optimum, and per-image adaptivity is complexity without commensurate payoff.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Object scale distributions vary hugely across images, so the single-resolution optimum overpays on most inputs by construction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one detector at three resolutions per image on a sample and histogram the minimal sufficient resolution; a spread distribution proves the headroom exists within a day.

title: Post-suppression instance-level distillation across detector architectures
one_line_idea: Distill the teacher's final post-suppression detections, its actual behavioral output, instead of intermediate feature maps, hypothesizing that behavior transfers across architectures where features cannot.
problem: Detection distillation matches intermediate features, which binds teacher and student to compatible architectures and transfers internal idiosyncrasies rather than the output behavior deployment actually cares about.
core_hypothesis: The teacher's post-suppression detection set is a cleaner, architecture-agnostic distillation target, and training students against it as soft ground truth with score-weighted matching outperforms feature distillation in cross-architecture settings.
core_claim: Behavioral distillation will beat feature distillation when teacher and student differ structurally, and match it when they are homologous, while being simpler to implement across arbitrary pairs.
method_sketch: Generate teacher detection sets with scores on unlabeled and labeled data, define a matching-based soft loss treating high-score teacher outputs as weighted pseudo ground truth, train heterogeneous students, and compare against feature-distillation and label-only baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: In cross-family teacher-student pairs, behavioral distillation will yield higher student metrics than feature alignment, with the advantage disappearing for same-family pairs.
why_important: Cross-architecture distillation is the practical route to fast deployable detectors as new architectures emerge faster than deployment stacks change.
why_possibly_novel: Output distillation exists in fragments, but a systematic post-suppression behavioral-distillation study across heterogeneous detector families appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Distill what the teacher does, not what it thinks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill one transformer teacher into one convolutional student via both routes at matched budgets and compare on one benchmark.
main_risk: Teacher errors in the detection set are inherited without the mitigating dark knowledge that feature maps might carry.
kill_risk: If feature distillation wins even in strongly heterogeneous pairs, internal representations carry irreplaceable signal and the behavioral route is inferior.
community_default_belief: Effective detection distillation requires matching intermediate representations, and output-level distillation discards most of the teacher's knowledge.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The dark-knowledge intuition was formed on classification logits, and its extrapolation to spatial feature maps across architectures is an unexamined assumption.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train one student on teacher detections as soft labels for a short schedule against a label-only control; an early gap indicates transferable behavioral signal quickly.

title: Per-region early exit for spatially adaptive detection compute
one_line_idea: Let easy regions of an image exit the detection network early while hard regions continue through deeper computation, making compute spatially adaptive within a single forward pass.
problem: Detection difficulty varies enormously within images, yet every pixel receives identical network depth, so uniform compute is misallocated relative to the spatial difficulty distribution.
core_hypothesis: Region difficulty is estimable from early-layer features reliably enough that per-region depth allocation preserves accuracy at a large average-compute saving, with exits calibrated to defer whenever uncertain.
core_claim: A per-region early-exit detector will trace a better accuracy-latency frontier than uniform-depth baselines and per-image early-exit variants across benchmarks and hardware-realistic latency measurement.
method_sketch: Attach detection sub-heads at intermediate depths, train exit-confidence estimators for regional predictions with deferral calibration, implement block-sparse continued computation for deferred regions, and profile real latency on target hardware.

minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement two exit points on one detector, calibrate deferral, and measure accuracy-latency frontiers on one benchmark with realistic batching.
main_risk: Block-sparse execution may achieve poor hardware utilization, letting theoretical savings evaporate in practice.
kill_risk: If early features cannot predict regional difficulty without frequent harmful commitments, deferral rates stay high and savings never materialize.
community_default_belief: Efficiency gains come from smaller or pruned models applied uniformly, since irregular spatial computation is hardware-hostile.

fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train a probe from early features to predict where a full model's detections concentrate; strong predictability justifies the architecture investment within days.

title: Error-cost-weighted compute allocation in detection cascades
one_line_idea: Allocate cascade compute according to deployment-specific class error costs, spending depth on high-stakes candidate detections instead of treating all candidates as equally worth refining.
problem: Detection cascades refine candidates by confidence alone, but deployments have wildly asymmetric error costs across classes, and compute allocation ignoring these costs is economically suboptimal at fixed budgets.
core_hypothesis: Routing candidates through refinement stages based on expected cost reduction, combining uncertainty with a class-cost matrix, yields lower total deployment cost than confidence-based routing at the same average compute.
core_claim: Cost-aware cascade routing dominates confidence-based routing on cost-weighted metrics across a range of realistic cost matrices without retraining the stage models.
method_sketch: Formulate routing as expected-cost-reduction maximization per candidate given stage-wise error models estimated on validation data, implement the router over an existing two-stage cascade, and evaluate across sampled cost matrices against confidence routing.
falsifiable_prediction: For asymmetric cost matrices, cost-aware routing will reduce total expected cost measurably at matched compute, converging to confidence routing only when costs are uniform.
why_important: It connects detection serving to decision theory, extracting deployment value from information that every operator has but no pipeline uses.
why_possibly_novel: Cascades and cost-sensitive learning are old separately; expected-cost-reduction routing for detection cascade compute appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Route compute by what mistakes cost, not by how unsure the model feels.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the router on one public cascade with two synthetic cost matrices and compare cost-weighted outcomes against confidence routing at equal compute.
main_risk: Stage-wise error models may be too inaccurate for expected-cost estimates to beat the simple confidence heuristic.
kill_risk: If cost-aware and confidence routing coincide across realistic cost matrices, uncertainty already proxies cost adequately and the machinery is redundant.
community_default_belief: Cascade routing by model confidence is effectively optimal, and error costs belong in post-hoc thresholding rather than in compute allocation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence ignores which class is at stake, so at fixed compute it necessarily over-refines cheap-error candidates and under-refines expensive-error ones under asymmetric costs.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulate routing decisions on cached cascade outputs under one asymmetric cost matrix; the cost gap between policies computes without any retraining in hours.

title: Objectness-peak-driven sparse high-resolution computation for small objects
one_line_idea: Run cheap dense low-resolution processing everywhere and expensive high-resolution feature extraction only in sparse neighborhoods of predicted objectness peaks, unifying accuracy and efficiency for small-object workloads.
problem: Small-object accuracy demands high-resolution features whose dense computation is prohibitively expensive, while the objects occupying those features cover a tiny fraction of the image area.
core_hypothesis: A two-scale design with sparse high-resolution patches gathered around low-resolution objectness peaks retains nearly all small-object accuracy of dense high-resolution processing at a small fraction of its cost.

method_sketch: Train a low-resolution branch emitting objectness peaks, gather high-resolution patches around peaks with a learned budget controller, fuse scales for final detection, and evaluate compute-accuracy tradeoffs against dense baselines on aerial and surveillance data.
falsifiable_prediction: On imagery where objects cover a small area fraction, the sparse system will retain the bulk of dense small-object average precision at a fraction of the multiply-accumulate cost, degrading gracefully as object coverage grows.
why_important: It could make high-resolution small-object detection affordable on edge hardware, where the applications that need it actually run.
why_possibly_novel: Related zoom and sparse-computation ideas exist; an integrated peak-gathered sparse high-resolution pipeline with budget control appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Dense awareness, sparse acuity: compute foveally like biological vision.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the two-scale pipeline on one aerial benchmark and compare small-object metrics and measured compute against dense high-resolution and plain low-resolution baselines.
main_risk: Peak misses at low resolution are unrecoverable downstream, capping the recall ceiling of the whole system.
kill_risk: If low-resolution objectness cannot reach high recall for small objects even at generous localization tolerance, the gathering premise collapses.
community_default_belief: Reliable small-object detection requires dense high-resolution processing; sparse shortcuts sacrifice exactly the targets of interest.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detecting that something is present is far easier than characterizing it, so a cheap low-resolution stage can plausibly achieve the near-perfect recall that the expensive stage then refines.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure recall of low-resolution objectness peaks against ground-truth small objects at loose matching on one dataset; the single recall number decides feasibility in a day.

title: Decomposing corruption robustness into localization and classification channels
one_line_idea: Decompose detection degradation under image corruptions into localization versus classification error growth, testing whether localization breaks first and needs its own robustness treatment.
problem: Corruption robustness for detection is reported as aggregate metric drops, hiding whether degradation comes from boxes drifting or labels flipping, though the two failure channels demand entirely different fixes.
core_hypothesis: Localization degrades earlier and faster than classification under common corruptions like blur and noise, implying that classification-centric robustness methods imported from image recognition address the smaller half of the detection problem.
core_claim: A channel-decomposed corruption study will show localization-dominant degradation profiles for a majority of corruption types, and localization-targeted robust training will recover more aggregate metric than classification-targeted equivalents.
method_sketch: Evaluate detectors across corruption suites while separately tracking box-quality distributions on matched objects and label-flip rates, then compare robustness interventions targeted at each channel under the decomposition.
falsifiable_prediction: For blur- and noise-type corruptions, box-quality decay on still-detected objects will exceed label-flip growth at matched severities, and localization-robust training will outperform classification-robust training on aggregate corrupted metrics.
why_important: The field imports robustness techniques from classification wholesale, and a channel decomposition would redirect effort to where detection actually breaks.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks exist for detection, but a systematic channel decomposition with intervention comparison appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ask which half of detection breaks under corruption before choosing the medicine.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one detector over one corruption suite logging matched-object box quality and label flips per severity, and plot the two degradation curves.
main_risk: Matching objects across clean and corrupted evaluations introduces its own methodology choices that could bias the decomposition.
kill_risk: If classification flips dominate everywhere, the localization-first hypothesis is wrong and existing classification-robustness transfer is vindicated.
community_default_belief: Corruption robustness is primarily a feature-invariance problem, and methods proven on classification transfer to detection without modification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Precise spatial regression plausibly depends on high-frequency information that corruptions destroy before semantic category information degrades.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare box-overlap distributions of matched detections at increasing blur on one dataset; localization decay is visible from cached outputs within a day.

title: Geographic appearance-prior audit with lightweight geo-adapters
one_line_idea: Audit per-class detection performance across geographic regions where the same category looks systematically different, and correct disparities with tiny region-conditioned adapters instead of full per-region models.
problem: Categories like taxis, houses, and street signs vary in appearance by region, and detectors trained on geographically skewed data likely underperform elsewhere, yet detection lacks systematic geographic disparity measurement or remediation.
core_hypothesis: Per-class geographic performance disparities are substantial and appearance-driven, and small adapter modules conditioned on coarse region identity recover most of the gap at a fraction of per-region model cost.
core_claim: A geographic audit will document class-specific disparities on region-tagged evaluation data, and geo-adapters will close a large share of the measured gaps without degrading source-region performance.
method_sketch: Assemble region-tagged evaluation subsets from existing geotagged datasets, measure per-class regional gaps, train adapter modules on modest regional data with the backbone frozen, and compare against fine-tuning and no-adaptation baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Regional gaps will be concentrated in appearance-variable classes rather than uniform across categories, and adapters will recover most of the gap for those classes with under a few percent added parameters.
why_important: Detection systems ship globally while being trained regionally, and unmeasured geographic disparity is both a product-quality and an equity problem.
why_possibly_novel: Geographic bias is documented for classification datasets; a class-resolved detection audit paired with an adapter remediation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The same class is a different-looking class elsewhere; treat geography as a first-class condition.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one detector on region-partitioned subsets of a geotagged dataset for a handful of appearance-variable classes and train adapters for the worst region.
main_risk: Region-tagged evaluation data may confound geography with camera, density, and annotation-practice differences.
kill_risk: If per-class regional gaps are small once confounds are controlled, the disparity problem is minor and adapters are unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Large-scale diverse training data makes detectors geographically general, and residual regional variation is negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web-scale data is heavily skewed toward specific regions, and appearance-defined categories inherit that skew directly into their decision boundaries.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare per-class metrics between two region partitions of an existing geotagged evaluation set; the gap table falls out of one evaluation run.

title: Isolating the camera-processing share of cross-camera detection degradation
one_line_idea: Quantify how much cross-camera detection degradation is caused by image signal processing differences rather than scene or optics change, and neutralize it with ISP-randomized augmentation or RAW-domain detection.
problem: Detectors degrade when deployed on new camera hardware even in similar scenes, and the community attributes this vaguely to domain gap without separating the controllable ISP component, denoising, sharpening, tone mapping, from genuine scene differences.
core_hypothesis: A large share of cross-camera degradation is attributable to ISP-induced statistical differences, and randomizing a parameterized ISP simulation during training removes most of that share cheaply.
core_claim: Controlled re-processing experiments will attribute a measurable fraction of cross-camera drop to ISP settings, and ISP-randomization training will recover most of that fraction on real cross-camera evaluations.
method_sketch: Reprocess RAW-available datasets through varied ISP pipelines to isolate the ISP effect on a frozen detector, train with parameterized ISP augmentation, and evaluate on genuinely different camera systems against standard augmentation baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: The same scenes reprocessed with different ISP settings will cause meaningful metric drops on frozen detectors, and ISP-randomized training will cut cross-camera degradation substantially relative to color-jitter-style baselines.
why_important: Camera heterogeneity is a constant of real deployments, and attributing then removing the controllable component converts a mystery gap into an engineering fix.
why_possibly_novel: ISP effects on downstream vision are noted in imaging literature, but a detection-focused attribution study with randomization training at deployment realism appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Split the domain gap into what the camera pipeline did and what the world did.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reprocess one RAW dataset under three ISP configurations, measure frozen-detector metric variation, and train one ISP-augmented model for cross-camera testing.
main_risk: RAW-available detection datasets are scarce, potentially forcing simulation-heavy approximations of ISP diversity.
kill_risk: If ISP reprocessing barely moves frozen-detector metrics, the ISP share of the gap is small and the augmentation targets a minor factor.
community_default_belief: Cross-camera degradation is an amorphous domain-shift problem to be handled by generic domain adaptation on deployment data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A camera pipeline applies deterministic, parameterizable transforms, and randomizing over that parameter space is a targeted, data-free intervention generic adaptation cannot match in cost.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run a frozen detector on one scene set processed by two very different ISP settings; the metric delta isolates the effect in a single day.

title: Spatial-consistency test-time adaptation designed for detection
one_line_idea: Adapt detectors at test time with an augmentation-consistency objective over spatial predictions, avoiding the entropy-minimization collapse that classification-derived adaptation methods suffer on detection outputs.
problem: Test-time adaptation methods built for classification, entropy minimization and prediction sharpening, misbehave on detection because false positives feed self-reinforcing loops and background dominates the output distribution.
core_hypothesis: Consistency of boxes and scores across geometric and photometric augmentations of the same test image is a shift-robust, collapse-resistant adaptation signal for detection, unlike entropy-style objectives.
core_claim: Augmentation-consistency adaptation will improve detection under shift where entropy-based adaptation degrades it, remaining stable over long adaptation streams without collapse safeguards.
method_sketch: At test time, process augmented views per image or batch, define a matched-prediction consistency loss over boxes and scores with background-dominance normalization, update only normalization and adapter parameters, and evaluate on corruption and real-shift streams against adaptation baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: On standard shift streams, consistency adaptation will produce monotone or stable gains while entropy-based baselines exhibit degradation or collapse episodes, with the gap widening over stream length.
why_important: Test-time adaptation is the only option when shifted labels are unavailable, and detection currently lacks a native, stable formulation of it.
why_possibly_novel: Test-time adaptation is heavily studied for classification; a detection-native consistency objective with stream-stability analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Adapt to what stays the same under augmentation, not to what makes scores sharper.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both objectives on one detector and one corruption stream, tracking metric trajectories over the stream to compare stability and gains.
main_risk: Per-image multi-view processing raises inference cost, which may be unacceptable in the latency-bound deployments that need adaptation most.
kill_risk: If consistency updates also drift toward degenerate solutions over long streams, the collapse-resistance claim fails and the approach joins the methods it criticizes.
community_default_belief: Test-time adaptation techniques validated on classification transfer to detection with minor engineering adjustments.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection outputs are dominated by background and structured spatially, violating the distributional assumptions that make entropy objectives sensible for classification.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run an entropy-based adaptation baseline on one detection corruption stream and check for degradation; documenting the failure mode motivates the alternative within days.

title: Scale-histogram matching to fix apparent-size distribution shift
one_line_idea: Diagnose deployment degradation caused purely by different object apparent-size distributions, camera mounted higher, wider lens, and fix it with scale-histogram-matched augmentation instead of full domain adaptation.
problem: A deployment whose camera geometry shifts object apparent sizes away from training statistics degrades even with identical scenes and classes, and this cheap-to-fix shift is bundled indistinguishably into generic domain-gap thinking.
core_hypothesis: Apparent-size distribution mismatch alone accounts for a meaningful share of camera-geometry deployment drops, and resampling training scales to match the deployment histogram recovers most of that share without any target-domain images beyond the histogram estimate.
core_claim: Scale-controlled experiments will isolate a pure size-shift effect, and histogram-matched rescaling augmentation will recover the majority of it at trivial cost using only unlabeled target data for histogram estimation.
method_sketch: Construct size-shifted evaluations by controlled resizing of standard datasets to isolate the effect, estimate deployment size histograms from unlabeled target detections, retrain or fine-tune with scale-resampled augmentation matching the target histogram, and evaluate on genuine cross-geometry data.
falsifiable_prediction: Frozen detectors will show clear metric drops on purely size-shifted data, and histogram-matched training will eliminate most of the drop while leaving other shift components untouched.
why_important: Camera geometry changes are among the most common deployment realities, and a one-knob statistical fix beats deploying heavyweight adaptation machinery for this component.
why_possibly_novel: Scale augmentation is universal, but deployment-histogram-matched scale resampling with an isolated size-shift attribution appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Match the size statistics the deployment will see, not a generic multi-scale prior.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a frozen detector on size-rescaled versions of its own test set to isolate the effect, then fine-tune with histogram matching for one simulated geometry change.
main_risk: Aggressive rescaling changes context and blur statistics as side effects, partially confounding the isolated size effect.
kill_risk: If standard multi-scale training already makes detectors invariant to realistic size-distribution shifts, the problem is pre-solved and the method redundant.
community_default_belief: Standard multi-scale augmentation confers sufficient scale invariance for realistic deployment geometry changes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multi-scale training optimizes average performance under a fixed size prior, which is different from matching a systematically displaced deployment prior.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Test a frozen detector on its test set uniformly rescaled by moderate factors; nontrivial metric drops demonstrate residual scale sensitivity immediately.

title: Artifact-adversarial filtering for diffusion-generated tail-class training instances
one_line_idea: Use generative inpainting to add tail-class instances to real scenes, but filter candidates through an artifact detector trained adversarially so models cannot learn generation artifacts as class features.
problem: Diffusion-inpainted training objects carry subtle generation artifacts, and detectors trained on them risk binding class identity to artifact signatures, inflating benchmark gains that collapse on real-world instances.
core_hypothesis: Artifact-shortcut learning is a real and measurable failure of generative augmentation for detection, and filtering or perturbing generated instances until an artifact discriminator is at chance removes the shortcut while preserving the augmentation benefit.
core_claim: Artifact-adversarial filtering will preserve most of the tail-class recall gains of generative augmentation while eliminating the real-versus-generated generalization gap that unfiltered augmentation exhibits.
method_sketch: Generate tail-class inpaintings, train a discriminator between real and generated crops, filter or regenerate until discriminability approaches chance, train detectors on filtered versus unfiltered augmentation, and evaluate on strictly real held-out tail instances.
falsifiable_prediction: Unfiltered augmentation will show a measurable gap between generated-instance and real-instance evaluation for the augmented classes, and filtering will close most of the gap at limited augmentation-volume cost.
why_important: Generative augmentation is rapidly becoming standard for rare classes, and an unaddressed artifact shortcut would corrupt tail progress claims across the field.
why_possibly_novel: Generative augmentation is common; discriminator-at-chance filtering as a shortcut-prevention criterion for detection augmentation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Augment only with fakes that a trained expert network cannot tell from real.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Augment three tail classes with and without filtering on one benchmark and compare real-instance evaluation gains and the real-versus-generated performance gap.
main_risk: Filtering may discard exactly the most useful diverse samples, trading shortcut removal against augmentation coverage.
kill_risk: If unfiltered augmentation shows no real-instance generalization gap, the artifact-shortcut concern is empirically unfounded and filtering is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Generated instances that look realistic to humans are safe training data for detection augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks exploit sub-perceptual statistical regularities, so human realism is an irrelevant safety criterion for shortcut formation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train a discriminator between generated and real crops of one class; high discriminator accuracy proves machine-visible artifacts exist and sizes the shortcut risk in a day.

title: Generative counterfactual hard negatives against context shortcuts
one_line_idea: Use generative editing to create near-boundary hard negatives, the object removed but its shadow, mount, or context kept, teaching detectors that context alone must not trigger detections.
problem: Detectors fire on contextual signatures, empty roads where cars belong, mounting poles without signs, because natural training data almost never contains context-present-object-absent counterexamples.
core_hypothesis: Systematically generated context-without-object negatives populate the undersampled side of the decision boundary and reduce context-driven false positives more per example than any natural negative mining can.
core_claim: Training with generative counterfactual negatives will cut context-triggered false positives substantially at matched recall, outperforming hard-negative mining from natural images at equal added-example budgets.
method_sketch: Remove annotated objects via inpainting while deliberately preserving shadows and contextual fixtures, add these as explicit background regions with elevated negative-loss weight, and evaluate context-triggered false positives on scene-only test imagery against mining baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained with counterfactual negatives will show a marked reduction in detections on object-free contexts while standard models fire regularly, with overall precision improving at fixed recall.
why_important: Context-triggered false positives are a signature failure of deployed detection in surveillance and driving, and natural data structurally cannot teach the correction.
why_possibly_novel: Inpainting-based augmentation exists for positives; deliberately artifact-controlled context-preserving negatives as boundary supervision appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Manufacture the training examples nature refuses to provide: the scene minus the object.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate counterfactual negatives for two context-prone classes, retrain one detector, and measure firing rates on verified object-free context imagery against the baseline.
main_risk: Inpainting residue could let models detect the edit rather than learn the semantic boundary, requiring artifact controls.
kill_risk: If baseline detectors rarely fire on object-free contexts to begin with, the shortcut is marginal and the augmentation solves little.
community_default_belief: False positives are best reduced by mining hard negatives from natural data at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Natural data barely contains the critical counterfactual configurations, so mining searches a distribution in which the needed examples are nearly absent.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure a frozen detector's firing rate on inpainted object-removed scenes; a substantial rate directly demonstrates the context shortcut within a day.

title: Capability-decomposed audit of synthetic-to-real detection transfer
one_line_idea: Measure synthetic-to-real transfer separately for localization, objectness ranking, and naming capabilities, replacing single-number domain-gap conclusions with a capability-resolved map of what synthetic data actually teaches.
problem: Synthetic detection data is judged by aggregate real-world metrics after fine-tuning, so the field cannot say which detection sub-capabilities transfer well from simulation and which require real data, leading to blanket over- or under-investment in simulation.
core_hypothesis: Detection sub-capabilities transfer from synthetic data at very different rates, with geometric capabilities like localization and objectness transferring far better than appearance-dependent naming, implying hybrid data strategies dominate uniform ones.
core_claim: A capability-decomposed evaluation of synthetic-pretrained models will show strong localization transfer and weak naming transfer, and a hybrid strategy, synthetic for geometry plus small real data for naming, will match much larger all-real budgets.
method_sketch: Pretrain on procedural or simulated scenes, evaluate frozen and fine-tuned models separately on class-agnostic proposal quality, ranking calibration, and naming accuracy on real benchmarks, then test hybrid data allocations against all-real baselines at matched cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Class-agnostic localization transfer from synthetic data will reach a large fraction of real-data performance while naming transfer remains poor, and the hybrid allocation will beat all-real training at matched total data cost.
why_important: Simulation investment decisions across autonomous driving, robotics, and industrial inspection currently rest on aggregate numbers that hide which capability the money buys.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic-to-real transfer is heavily studied in aggregate; a standardized capability-decomposed audit with hybrid-allocation consequences appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ask what simulation teaches, capability by capability, instead of whether it works overall.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain one detector on an existing synthetic corpus, measure the three capability transfers on one real benchmark, and run one hybrid-versus-all-real comparison at matched budget.
main_risk: Capability metrics are entangled in end-to-end architectures, requiring careful probe design to keep the decomposition honest.
kill_risk: If all capabilities transfer equally poorly or equally well, the decomposition adds no allocation-relevant information.
community_default_belief: Synthetic-to-real transfer quality is a single domain-gap property of the simulator, improved by making rendering more photorealistic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Geometry is cheap to simulate correctly while appearance statistics are hard, so transfer should be capability-structured, making photorealism the wrong investment for the capabilities that already transfer.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate class-agnostic proposal recall on real data for any existing synthetic-trained detector versus its naming accuracy; a large asymmetry validates the decomposition premise immediately.
